title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
abstract: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.

title: Generative AI and the Evolution of Mortgage Underwriting: Measuring and Mitigating Racial Disparities
abstract: Abstract Mortgage underwriting is entering a new phase of technological change as general-purpose generative AI tools begin to appear in mortgage origination workflows. We develop an audit framework to evaluate how large language models process mortgage applications. Using real HMDA applications, we experimentally manipulate borrower race, race proxies, and credit quality, and prompt leading commercial LLMs to make approval and pricing recommendations. LLMs recommend more denials and higher interest rates for Black applicants than otherwise identical white applicants, with disparities largest for riskier loans and persisting when race is signaled through names or locations. A simple instruction to avoid bias substantially reduces disparities when race is explicit, partially reduces the name-based pricing gap, and does little against the geographic pricing gap. In matched HMDA–Freddie Mac data, race-blind LLM recommendations correlate with actual lender pricing and subsequent delinquency, though the delinquency association operates largely through observed credit scores. The results show how AI auditing can inform mortgage underwriting governance before general-purpose models become more deeply embedded in origination workflows.

title: RETR: A Structure-Preserving RGB-Event Transformer for Robust 3D Lane Detection
abstract: Robust 3D lane detection requires accurate metric road geometry recovery from visual inputs, yet conventional RGB-based approaches suffer from fragile lane evidence under adverse illumination, motion blur, and long-range perspective compression. Event cameras offer complementary high-temporal-resolution, high dynamic-range structural cues that are robust to these challenges, but their sparse, motion-dependent responses cannot be directly fused into consistent 3D geometry. In this paper, we present the first attempt to introduce event cameras into 3D lane detection. To enable systematic research, we first build two multimodal benchmarks with metric 3D lane annotations: DSEC-3DLD (real-world sequences) and Ev-OpenLane (large-scale simulated sequences). We further propose RETR, a structure preserving transformer that converts complementary RGB and event observations into coherent 3D lane geometry. RETR first aligns modality consistent evidence through Reciprocal Context Flow Fusion, then preserves thin and uncertain lane structures with Uncertainty Aware Structural Consolidation, and finally decodes ordered lane hypotheses using a Geometry State Decoder with proposal conditioned initialization, reference conditioned query evolution, and diversified geometric inquiry. Extensive experiments show that RETR achieves state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks, especially showing strong improvements in challenging lighting and complex road geometry scenarios. Code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/duskswell/RETR.

title: FDAM: A Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Pavement Crack Grid Localization
abstract: Pavement crack grid localization remains challenging for thin and tiny cracks due to weak visual cues and background interference. Box detection often misses these cracks, while supervised semantic segmentation faces limited pixel-wise annotations and high labeling costs. In this paper, we propose a Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task framework (FDAM) with box detection and grid classification branches. The core grid classification branch comprises Frequency-Domain Enhancement (FDE) and Directional Feature Refinement (DFR). FDE adaptively weights spectral bands and fuses reconstructed features with spatial features. DFR captures thin crack patterns through multi-scale strip convolutions, direction-sensitive modulation, and feature recalibration. Sparse positive cells and ambiguous local predictions motivate adaptive grid supervision. Adaptive Importance Reweighting emphasizes uncertain predictions and local label transitions, with focal supervision for all cells. Our contribution is to couple the box detection and grid classification branches through shared feature learning for pavement crack grid localization. We validate FDAM on our RoadDistress2026 dataset of thin and tiny cracks and further evaluate it on public datasets Crack500 and DeepCrack. The code is available at https://github.com/Lab-PANbin/FDAM

title: Architecting the Corporate AI Infrastructure: The Evolving Roles of AI Governance Committees and Chief Ethics Officers
abstract: The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into core business operations has created an urgent need for robust corporate governance infrastructures capable of managing complex ethical, legal, and operational risks. While organizations have increasingly adopted high-level AI ethics principles, a critical implementation gap persists: fewer than half of organizations that cite AI governance as a boardroom priority have a formalized governance framework in place. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a structured corporate AI governance architecture (CAIGA) centred on two mutually reinforcing pillars. First, it examines the evolving mandate of specialized C-suite roles, specifically Chief Privacy Officers (CPOs) and Chief Ethics Officers (ChEOs), in formalizing accountability for AI usage across the enterprise. Second, it argues that cross-functional AI Governance Committees, uniting representatives from legal, technology, data science, cybersecurity, and business units, are the essential organizational mechanism for translating ethical principles into operational decisions, including strategic go/no-go approvals for new AI initiatives. Drawing on a conceptual review of peer-reviewed governance literature, regulatory frameworks including the EU AI Act, and documented industry practice, this paper contributes a replicable governance architecture that embeds clear accountability policies, structured risk management workflows, and an organization-wide ethical AI culture. The framework is illustrated through application to the financial services sector. The findings have direct implications for corporate leaders, risk professionals, and policymakers navigating the rapidly evolving global AI regulatory landscape.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
abstract: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.

title: When AI Agents Should Repair, Replan, or Abandon: A Threshold Theory of Plan Commitment
abstract: AI agents often discover mid-execution that their plan is broken, for example when an action fails or a tool is withdrawn. Deployed systems use conventions such as retry loops or "always replan," and a recent benchmark finds no fixed strategy dominates. This paper derives the optimal policy. In the model, a disruption destroys the causal support of part of a plan; repair is a partial reset that preserves the plan's structure, replanning is a full reset, and changing a plan is costly because others have conditioned on it. The optimal policy is a threshold in effective disruption depth: repair shallow damage, replan after deep damage, and abandon the goal when even a fresh plan is not worth its cost. Depth depends on plan structure. In expectation, a single broken action forces 1+R(G)/n actions to be revalidated, where R(G) counts the pairs of actions joined by a dependency path; to first order, a fully serial plan switches to replanning at raw damage about w times smaller than a plan of w parallel chains. A closed-form stability-price threshold determines when a worse repaired plan should be kept over a better fresh one. As language-model planners push replanning costs toward zero, the stability price becomes the only force sustaining plan commitment. Under repeated disruptions, revision frictions make commitment hysteresis optimal: the agent keeps executing a plan it would never choose fresh, and each repair adds patch debt until the debt outweighs repair's cost advantage and the agent rebuilds. A value-of-diagnosis result states when measuring damage is worth its compute and shows that "always replan" is optimal when damage is predictably deep and replanning is the better fallback. A separately implemented numerical checker tests each proposition (zero violations; 1.6 million static-model evaluations), and the model's regime map reproduces that benchmark's regime flips qualitatively.

title: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
abstract: Micro-dramas (duanju) are reshaping digital production and consumption, yet a lack of longitudinal data connecting series to their platform visibility persists, limiting our understanding of the emerging medium. We introduce HongguoTrending, a longitudinal, multimodal dataset of hourly snapshots from seven trending lists of Hongguo, China's largest micro-drama platform. Collected through a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the archive links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, cover images, sampled episode videos, and audience engagement metrics. Exploratory analyses show distinct turnover rates between web and mobile trending lists, production-driven mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong associations between user sharing and next-day rank gains. Accessible via a RESTful API, this dataset supports empirical research on algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture.

title: CONTEXT-PCa: Evaluating the role of clinical context in MRI-based AI for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (study protocol)
abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the role of clinical variables - their breadth, source, and quality - in the development, utility, and generalisability of an AI system for bi-parametric MRI (bpMRI)-based diagnosis of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). Clinical context is added to the published PI-CAI-2B image-only model, whose weights are fixed. The study cohort comprises 6,022 biparametric MRI cases from 4,540 patients at University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (2019-2024), of which 4,834 cases (3,632 patients) are held out for internal testing. Forty-three clinical variables are drawn from structured health records, clinical letters, MRI reports, and automated image measurements. The primary endpoint is the difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) between the image-context and image-only models on the internal test set. Secondary analyses compare combining strategies, the contribution of individual variables, and performance across subgroups. All models are further tested on five external cohorts from primary diagnosis and population-based screening.

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

title: When Does Label-Free Deconfounding of Document Embeddings Work?
abstract: Document embeddings encode spurious attributes that can distort semantic comparisons; yet supervised erasure requires metadata that is often unavailable. We systematically investigate label-free deconfounding across corpora and embedding models. Our results show that label-free methods improve semantic utility over unprocessed embeddings, while simple geometric approaches recover much of the supervised benefit, sometimes matching metadata-supervised erasure in linear confounder recoverability and semantic utility. We identify two distinct causes of ineffective erasure: poor proxy-confounder alignment and insufficient intervention coverage. Crucially, confounder recoverability and semantic utility are distinct dimensions of deconfounding success: utility can improve despite residual confounder information, while stronger suppression does not necessarily improve utility. Moreover, reduced linear recoverability can coexist with substantial nonlinear recoverability. Together, these findings distinguish confounder discovery from intervention effectiveness and highlight the importance of evaluating nuisance suppression alongside semantic preservation.

title: Using machine learning approaches to classify false-positives generated by static analysis tools - An empirical study using small datasets
abstract: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools are vital for software development to reduce the cost and time required for manual code reviews. It was established in our previous study that the best tools reported in the software engineering community return high false-positive and false-negative rates when used for code analysis. Several approaches have been taken in existing studies to identify false-positive alarms generated by SCA tools, in helping to enhance the utility of these tools. However, existing studies reveal several limitations, chiefly among which is the tendency to focus on a limited number of alarm types or failing to evaluate a large breadth of Machine-Learning (ML) techniques comprehensively. This study has addressed this opportunity. We identified the best Code Representation Learning (CRL) techniques and ML algorithms for identifying false-positives, where results show that performance outcomes vary based on the characteristics of the training datasets and the goal of the model building. Given the evidence established in this study, we recommend further investigations targeting specific configurations of advanced CRLs and ML Algorithms, including simple ML models.

title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

title: Assume/Guarantee Contracts for the Compositional Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Heterogeneous Teams
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems for heterogeneous teams require agents to collaborate to complete team tasks while making the best use of diverse agent capabilities. We introduce assume/guarantee contracts for heterogeneous multi-agent systems (AGC-MAS) and Iterative Heterogeneous Assignment for MARL (IHA-MARL). AGC-MAS contracts are compositional objects that encode the assumptions provided to, and the guarantees required of, each subtask contributing to the overall team task. We formulate contracts as tuples that specify a subtask, an automaton, timeout and success-probability requirements, and dispatch behavior. The automaton tracks an agent's high-level progress through the subtask associated with its contract and provides a natural mechanism for synchronization across contracts. Our abstraction enables robust interaction across heterogeneous low-level subtask implementations, allows heterogeneous agents to substitute for one another in satisfying contracts, and supports reuse of previously satisfied contracts in new team contexts. Having defined our theoretical framework, we develop a decomposition algorithm that breaks down a team task into a set of contracts. We then propose an iterative algorithm for task assignment and MARL that alternates between assigning contracts representing subtasks to individual agents, training the assigned agents to satisfy their contracts, and assessing their resulting capabilities to inform the next round of task assignments until the team's success probability meets the desired threshold. Our experimental results demonstrate the versatility of contracts in enabling agent substitution and contract reuse. Across three benchmarks with five seeds each, IHA-MARL achieves observed $100\%$ final evaluation success. In CPU timing pilots, comparable baselines required approximately $7$--$11\times$ more training-loop time.

title: Constrained Actionable Counterfactual Explanations With Economic Cost Optimization for Algorithmic Recourse in Credit Scoring Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Automated credit scoring increasingly relies on black‐box models, raising concerns about transparency and the right to algorithmic recourse under the EU AI Act and GDPR. Counterfactual explanations answer ‘what should change for a different outcome?’, yet existing methods often change immutable attributes such as age or gender, or ignore the heterogeneous economic costs of feature changes. This paper introduces CA‐CF (Constrained Actionable Counterfactual Explanations), a gradient‐based framework that jointly optimizes validity, proximity, economic cost and plausibility. CA‐CF projects each optimization step onto the feasible set defined by an immutable/hard‐actionable/soft‐actionable taxonomy. We prove that this projection is exact, that it rules out constraint violations at every iteration, that the projected subgradient method converges to critical points of the non‐smooth objective and that a preventive gradient mask is redundant. The cost combines and penalties, with weights elicited from experts or learned from data as a differentiable percentile cost. We evaluate CA‐CF on four datasets (German Credit, Give Me Some Credit, Credit Risk and Adult Census) against MIP‐ and DiCE‐based baselines and nine further methods in the CARLA library (308,574 counterfactuals, seed–fold protocol). Projection‐based variants achieve zero immutable and hard‐actionable violations, and CA‐CF delivers recourse at up to lower economic cost than DiCE‐random with a median latency of 11–34 ms. In CARLA, it is one of only two methods that are always successful and always feasible. A confidence margin cuts recourse invalidated by retraining from up to to at most . A post hoc sparsification step cuts the number of changed features by up to at no loss of validity. We report the limits: recourse for tree ensembles is sound and, with query‐based repair, valid in of cases rather than guaranteed and plans lie close to the decision boundary.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
abstract: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $dσ^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $σ^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
abstract: Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

title: SearchChord: Prompt Preselection and Field Recomposition for One-Step Image Editing
abstract: Finding effective prompts and seeds for one-step image editors requires balancing edit fidelity, source preservation, and computational cost. To address this challenge, we explore a large collection of candidate edits, where each candidate is defined by a unique prompt-seed pair, and generate corresponding images on demand. We present SearchChord, a training-free framework that leverages a large pool of such candidates, combining text-based preselection, image verification, and latent-field recomposition. Our ablation studies across pool sizes up to 200 candidates show that a pool of 100 offers a cost-effective operating point. Compared with feeding all 100 candidates into recomposition, TextSim preselects a subset of 10 candidates. Rather than uniform averaging, we incorporate image-verifier scores to weight each candidate during recomposition. Experiments on PIE-Bench and the proposed CropWeed-EditBench reveal a trade-off: candidate selection improves target-text alignment, while recomposition better preserves unmodified source content. The oracle verifier achieves the best performance in both preservation and target-text alignment. Practical verification partially recovers semantic alignment, but recomposition still compromises edit fidelity, including in agricultural image edits. These results motivate text-first preselection and stronger verification to balance preservation, fidelity, and cost. Code and data will be made publicly available.

title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
abstract: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

title: The Geometry of Conceptors in Neural-Activation Spaces
abstract: Conceptors represent concepts as graded collections of directions in neural-activation space rather than as single vectors. We develop a geometric account of how these representations depend on the contrast used to define a concept: opposing values in bipolar fitting, or presence and absence in unipolar fitting. We derive an exact decomposition of a centered pooled conceptor into an average pole filter, a mean-separation update, and a covariance-shape update. Experiments across five language models on sentiment, political leaning and stance, and depression expression show that both updates improve reconstruction of held-out contrasts. Additional directions preserve variation beyond the mean-difference line, and changing the comparator changes the benefit of these directions. Shape, size, and overlap each show up downstream: in amplification experiments, bipolar fits raise evidence for both poles more consistently than unipolar fits; conceptor size (the quota) correlates positively with layerwise probe performance; and cross-concept overlap quantifies interference under subspace removal, linking shared directions to Boolean composition. In an additional generation evaluation, conceptor filters achieve higher target-expression win rates against an unsteered reference than three mean-based controls. Together, these findings explain how fitting choices shape conceptor geometry and support bipolar fitting when the objective is to amplify both opposing poles.

title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
abstract: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

title: HybridQC: Hardware-Grounded Simulation of Tightly Integrated Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical performance depends on how quantum processors share classical compute, controllers, memory, and communication links. Circuit simulators and provider measurements expose kernel and job behavior, but leave topology-level questions about controller bottlenecks, quantum capacity, and mixed-workload contention unanswered. We present HybridQC, a discrete-event simulator for configurable hybrid compute units (HCUs). Users specify resource graphs containing classical compute, memory, controllers, quantum annealing (QA) and digital quantum computing (DQC) devices, and links. Jobs become dependent stages for preparation, quantum execution, transfers, reconstruction, and postprocessing. Finite capacities and selectable scheduling policies determine where stages wait and overlap. Service profiles use measurements from D-Wave Advantage 1 and Advantage 2 and IBM Kingston, Marrakesh, and Fez, separating physical quantum-processor occupancy from cloud wall time. Mean absolute percentage errors are 3.92%-8.04% for D-Wave access time and 5.26%-19.01% for IBM quantum seconds. Balanced 10x HCU scaling improves makespan by 2.19x-3.42x, while policy choice changes makespan by 1.80x for a mixed workload with 20 jobs per workload family. Scaling depends on which inputs grow: 100x data growth yields median runtime near 306 s, while 100x joint growth in circuits, shots, and depth reaches 4.806 x 10^7 s on the fixed HCU. HybridQC enables designers to study topology, scheduling, and workload growth before tightly integrated quantum-classical machines exist physically.

title: Political stance detection on X during the 2024 U.S. election: a comparative study of classical, neural, and transformer models
abstract: Abstract As online social networks (OSNs) play an increasingly influential role in political communication, accurately detecting political stance from noisy, short-form content remains a significant challenge in computational social science (CSS). This paper presents a controlled comparison of text classification models for political stance detection during the 2024 U.S. presidential election, focusing on candidate affiliation toward Donald Trump and Joe Biden–Kamala Harris. Using nearly 100,000 posts from X, we define candidate affiliation as a three-class target variable (Trump, Biden–Kamala, or Neutral) and use topic modeling to support keyword development and thematic characterization. Under a unified preprocessing, labeling, and evaluation pipeline, we compare classical machine learning models, sentence-embedding-based neural architectures, and a domain-adapted transformer. Results suggest that task-aligned text representation accounts for most of the predictive signal in this setting. While fine-tuned BERTweet achieves the strongest in-domain performance, carefully engineered classical models, particularly linear support vector machines, remain highly competitive. Multi-feature and ablation analyses further indicate that expanded metadata did not yield reliable gains beyond strong text representations. Overall, this work provides a controlled comparison of text models for candidate affiliation on a heuristically labeled corpus.

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
abstract: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
abstract: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

title: Beyond the Training Cameras: Coverage-Controlled Probes of Viewing Direction in Frozen Vision Models
abstract: Vision models are trained on 2D images of a 3D world. Do their hidden features encode the direction from which the camera views a scene, and if so, in what form? We study the relative viewing direction $α$ of two objects in rendered scenes where both object centres stay at fixed pixels while the camera moves, so that perspective, shading and shadows change but the projected layout does not. In eight pretrained models, from diffusion models to self-supervised and image-text encoders, $α$ is encoded in a strikingly simple form: a single two-dimensional plane in the hidden space, shared across scenes, in which the difference between the two objects' features traces $(\cosα, \sinα)$. The plane keeps its orientation when lighting, colours, floors and object shapes change. This encoding is more than a summary of a few visible measurements: readouts fitted on one set of camera paths stay accurate at camera positions outside their range in seven of the eight models, whereas decoders of the measured object and shadow geometry, equally accurate within that range, fail there. In the diffusion transformer PixArt-$α$, the plane forms abruptly at a single block and carries direction information to later blocks, yet editing it changes the objects rather than the generated viewpoint. We also examine how this encoding carries over to scanned real objects.

title: A Think Block Is Conditioning, Not a Plan
abstract: Generative models increasingly write a chain of thought before drawing, and report large gains from doing so. We ask what that text contributes, by substitution rather than ablation: holding the generator, sampler and seeds fixed, we replace the think block with controlled alternatives and measure the image. Across a unified model with a think mode, a reinforcement-learned reasoning generator, and a planner driving a frozen diffusion model, the same picture emerges. Content-free prose of matched length is worth nothing or less ($-0.05$ to $-0.15$). One sentence from an unrelated 8B model, naming the subject and a few identifying details, matches the generator's own plan in three to six times fewer conditioning tokens. The value sits where the referent is in doubt: writing down a name is worth $+0.33$ when it is right and $+0.05$ when it is wrong, and where the generator already succeeds the whole effect is $-0.07 \pm 0.07$. Cutting a plan at the text encoder's window leaves 272 of 286 images byte-identical, and a plan rewritten to fit that window ties a bare identification ($+0.003 \pm 0.044$), so a plan contains nothing the identification does not already supply. Field-level interventions find only colour executed reliably, and a control writing the same sentences into the user prompt shows that limit belongs to the generator rather than to the planning channel. Two judges and two annotators replicate the central contrasts. A think block earns its keep as a specification of what to draw, not as a plan that is carried out.

Field-level interventions find only colour executed reliably, and a control writing the same sentences into the user prompt shows that limit belongs to the generator rather than to the planning channel. Two judges and two annotators replicate the central contrasts. A think block earns its keep as a specification of what to draw, not as a plan that is carried out.

title: A Fast Algorithm for the Familywise Loss
abstract: The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in $O(K)$ time, where $K$ is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Financial Foundation Models: A Survey
abstract: Financial foundation models increasingly support workflows spanning financial question answering, disclosure analysis, forecasting, and decision-making. In these settings, uncertainty may concern whether evidence is valid and available at the relevant time, whether an interpretation is justified, which outcomes remain plausible, or which action is preferred under costs and risk constraints. Because these objects arise at different points in a workflow, uncertainty cannot be reduced to confidence in a final output. We introduce a source-aware framework that distinguishes six sources of uncertainty across evidence and context, model and inference, and outcome and action, while treating agentic workflows as the execution layer through which uncertainty can propagate, change form, or be reduced. We develop a mechanism-based taxonomy grounded in how methods construct or verify uncertainty and reliability representations, and use it to assess their applicability across financial task domains. We further map finance-specific empirical studies across the taxonomy and task domains to characterize the current research landscape. Our analysis shows that most reviewed studies address uncertainty in individual parts of financial workflows, with limited work connecting evidence and reasoning reliability to downstream prediction and constrained action. By connecting where uncertainty arises, how it is represented, and how it bears on downstream decisions, this survey provides a unified foundation for studying and evaluating uncertainty in financial foundation models.

title: Data underlaying chapter 7 to the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'
abstract: Research data for Chapter 7 in the dissertation 'Expanding Regulatory Sandboxes: Exploring institutional dynamics of hydrogen market development and governance in the Netherlands'The chapter title is: Serious Gaming and agent-based modelling as a proof of concept for virtual regulatory sandboxes The research objective is to establish a practical approach for using serious gaming as a structured behavioral data eleicitation method, to support ABM development. Through a case study, the pratcical approach is illustrated. This involved the execution of 12 serious game sessions (the hychain serious game) and the collection of behavioral and institutional mechanisms. The collection took place through observation, recording and transcription of each session and the analysis of the collected rules for the number of occurrences. The collected data and corresponding analysis are presented in the attached file. The attached file specifies the data of the game session, the governmental strategy in the session, the corresponding round, the governmental decision taken, the decisions made by actors, the interactions taking place, the individuals involved and a description of the decision or interaction.

title: Floorplan-Context-Aware Cross-Environment Human Activity Recognition from mmWave Radar Point Clouds
abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) models based on mmWave radar point clouds and trained in controlled open spaces often experience performance degradation when deployed in furnished rooms. We propose a Floorplan-Context-Aware (FCA) HAR enhancement method that augments the input with subject-furniture relative position information to improve cross-environment performance. Because existing mmWave point-cloud datasets lack registered floorplans, we introduce a pseudo-landmark augmentation strategy for training the FCA model. In cross-environment evaluation on the mm-ADL-Home dataset, FCA achieves 77.70% accuracy and 65.49% macro-F1, improving upon the point-cloud-only direct-transfer baseline by 10.73 and 10.05 percentage points, respectively, and exceeding the strongest evaluated adaptation baseline by 7.37 and 6.27 percentage points. At deployment, FCA requires only a one-time registration of furniture landmarks, with no target-domain activity annotations or model weight updates.

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

title: Policy Optimization With Multiple Verifiers via Pareto Rankings
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models. In tasks such as code generation and instruction following, multiple verifiers evaluate whether a response satisfies different requirements. Their outcomes provide detailed feedback about partial success, yet this feedback is commonly aggregated into a scalar reward for policy optimization. Rewarding only complete success discards distinctions among partial solutions, while counts and weighted sums impose comparisons between responses that satisfy different subsets of requirements. We introduce Partial-Order Likelihood Policy Optimization (POLPO), which learns from the comparisons established by verification without first constructing an aggregate reward. Pareto dominance identifies responses that satisfy additional requirements without losing any already satisfied, while leaving responses with conflicting outcomes incomparable. POLPO extends the listwise likelihood underlying Direct Preference Optimization by maximizing the total probability of all complete rankings consistent with these partial orders. This objective provides supervision from verified improvements even before complete solutions are available, without requiring a prescribed ordering of incomparable responses. Experiments on code generation and instruction following demonstrate improved learning efficiency and higher rates of complete requirement satisfaction compared with scalar-reward training. These results support partial-order likelihood as an effective approach to learning from multiple verifiers.

title: Faithfulness Under Pressure: Evaluating Hallucination Detectors for Financial RAG
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used in financial applications where generated answers must be grounded in specific documents, filings, or disclosures. Yet even with relevant context, answers may contradict, overextend, or misinterpret the supplied evidence. This paper presents a comparative study of intrinsic hallucination detection for financial RAG, where the task is to determine whether an answer is faithful to a supplied question–context pair. We evaluate DSPy-based prompt optimization, fine-tuned detectors, encoder-based detectors, and LLM-as-Judge frameworks across public benchmarks and finance-specific settings. To examine finance-specific behavior, we construct FinDER-HD, a balanced hallucination-detection benchmark derived from FinDER by synthesizing unfaithful counterparts for faithful financial question–context–answer examples. We further evaluate filing-scale robustness on PHANTOM, which varies context length, evidence position, and filing type. Results show that detector performance varies substantially across datasets, financial topics, reasoning types, and context regimes. DSPy-based prompt optimization is competitive under limited supervision, but robustness differs markedly by optimization strategy: demonstration-heavy methods perform strongly in short contexts yet degrade more sharply as context grows, whereas COPRO and especially GEPA remain substantially more stable. Selected LLM-as-Judge methods also perform strongly in finance-specific settings, but their operating behavior depends on threshold choice and prediction bias. These findings motivate deployment-oriented evaluation of financial RAG guardrails beyond aggregate F1, including finance-specific robustness, filing-scale stress testing, prediction bias, threshold calibration, and context-window feasibility.

title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.

title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

title: Log-optimal two-sample testing by betting
abstract: For each standard Borel observation space, we construct a single anytime-valid two-sample procedure that is asymptotically log-optimal for every pair of unknown probability laws and every limiting ratio of diverging sample sizes, including zero and infinity. For independent balanced pairs, the optimal log-wealth rate is $2\JS(P,Q)$, where $\JS$ is the Jensen--Shannon divergence. Unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen--Shannon information and the one-sample limit $\log W(n_1,n_2)/n_2\to\KL(Q\|P)$ when $n_1/n_2\to\infty$. Refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels provide universal constructions. Our main contribution is the generality of our construction, and its connections to classical batch efficiency notions. Practical implementations allow continuous classifier fine-tuning, as demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Adapting Reusable Reasoning Structures from Recurring Financial Events
abstract: Forecasting real-world events requires reasoning under uncertainty from information available at a fixed cutoff. Recent work has improved how large language models (LLMs) retrieve evidence and produce probabilistic forecasts, but each question is treated independently even when similar events recur. Resolved occurrences carry experience for later forecasts, yet past outcomes and case summaries do not preserve the relationships that made an earlier occurrence informative. We develop ReFoRM (Recurrent-event Forecasting with Reasoning Memory), which organizes reasoning from resolved events into predictive paths, retrieves relevant paths for a later occurrence, and reconstructs their relations using evidence at the new forecast cutoff. We evaluate ReFoRM on the Recurring Financial Events Set, which contains 300 questions across 40 recurring financial event families and uses earlier occurrences as hindsight for 100 forecast targets. Across five LLMs and six baselines, ReFoRM improves categorical and probabilistic forecasting performance. Further analyses show that validating historical relations with current evidence and reconstructing them enhances forecasting. Reasoning evaluation also demonstrates stronger evidence grounding, logical validity, and mechanism specificity.

title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

title: Large Language Models for AI Infrastructure
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to design, optimize, and operate the infrastructure behind AI training and serving, yet the literature remains fragmented across hardware design, machine learning systems, electronic design automation, and high-performance computing. We present a comprehensive survey of LLM-assisted AI infrastructure across its lifecycle, from accelerator design and kernel engineering to compilation, deployment, operations, data management, and energy optimization. We organize the literature by the primary resource the LLM manages: artifact-centric methods for computational artifacts, operational-centric methods for deployment context and system state, and resource-centric methods for data and energy. These categories span the lifecycle and cover AI-specific concerns such as distributed-training configuration, inference serving, GPU-cluster scheduling, and data loading. Building on this taxonomy, we conduct a cross-study quantitative synthesis of reported results. Because studies adopt heterogeneous benchmarks, baselines, hardware, and metrics, we compare methods only where evaluation conditions permit and align results along common dimensions: functional correctness, execution performance, throughput, resource and energy consumption, operational outcomes, and optimization cost, keeping each result's native metric, baseline, and setting rather than collapsing them into a single score. This comparison reveals where LLM-driven methods yield consistent gains, how reported gains in workload orchestration depend on the evaluation environment, from simulators to real clusters and production, and where evidence is still lacking. Together, the taxonomy, lifecycle perspective, and quantitative evaluation provide an evidence-grounded reference for LLM-driven engineering of AI infrastructure.

title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
abstract: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

title: Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators
abstract: Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

title: High-dimensional limit theorems for adaptive variants of SGD I: Ballistic limits
abstract: We develop the high-dimensional effective dynamics for adaptive, momentum-based variants of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). These effective dynamics are given by a Markov process. They key observation is that the non-Markovianity in the algorithm due to the exponential moving average and preconditioning can be treated using the method of averaging. Our approach applies to a broad class of algorithms including to Adaptive momentum estimation (ADAM), Momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schultz (MUON), and its variants. It also applies to a broad class of learning tasks, such at tensor PCA, Gaussian projective models, teacher-student networks, and a multi-layer neural network trained on the XOR problem using a hybrid of MUON and ADAM as commonly done in practice. We demonstrate how to this technique can give precise, quantitative comparisons between algorithms. In particular, we find interesting phenomena, such as the cross-over phenomenon where online SGD has better generalization than ADAM early in training until the learning curves cross and ADAM dominates. Furthermore, we prove a version of the Edge of Stability phenomenon. In particular, we introduce an analogue of the infinity Laplacian that sharply characterizes the Edge of Stability.

title: EntangledEdge: A Distributed System for Orbital Quantum Sensing and Learning
abstract: An orbital quantum sensor is more precise than classical and holds its information in a quantum state's superposition and entanglement, which classical measurement collapses. Learning on quantum-sensed data therefore requires a distributed system in which the data stay quantum from sensor to inference. We present EntangledEdge, the first system architecture to unify orbital quantum sensing and learning end-to-end, with a quantum data plane and a classical control plane. It routes each event to a channel-matched model in a capacity-diverse bank, adapts its detection threshold without labels, and aggregates across stations by hardware fidelity. Evaluated with a hybrid prototype (real quantum processors, simulated orbit-to-ground link) over satellite telemetry, EntangledEdge achieves high-quality inference at bounded per-event cost, improves quantum processor utilization, and scales with fleet size.

title: Where slide-level foundation-model classifiers fail on atypical breast lesions
abstract: Whether a ductal breast lesion is called atypical hyperplasia or low-grade carcinoma in situ increasingly determines surgery. However, slide-level classifiers built on pathology foundation models (PFMs) perform worst on these lesions. Using four PFMs, cross-validation on BRACS and preregistered hypotheses, we studied where the classification of atypia fails. Because slides are labelled with their most severe lesion, only 39% of the slides with annotated atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) were labelled ADH. Attention ranked the lesion high but rarely first, and showing the model only the lesion helped little, whereas classifiers trained per decision with lesion-level labels improved all four atypical boundaries. ADH regions inserted into benign slides raised the probability of malignancy more than that of atypia. In a hospital with pathologist-labelled single-subtype slides and in HISTAI, benign slides were scored closer to lesions and triage specificity fell from 0.48-0.53 to 0.00-0.07 and 0.22.

title: Unlocking Fine-Grained Cell Representations via Soft-Interior Rim Dense-Grid Pooling in Pathology Foundation Models
abstract: Fine-grained cell representations are essential for characterizing cellular heterogeneity and tissue organization in computational pathology. Pathology foundation models (PFMs) provide powerful pretrained features for transferable tissue analysis. HoVer-Net uses task-trained segmentation and typing, whereas CellViT++ averages native-grid tokens assigned to detected nuclei. However, the former requires cell-specific training; the latter ignores fractional nuclear coverage and can mix nuclear content with neighbouring tissue. Therefore, we propose SRDP, short for Soft-interior Rim Dense-grid Pooling, a training-free geometry-aware readout. We apply the frozen patch projection at half stride, interleave four offset lattices, map the cell mask to fractional coverage weights, and concatenate whole-cell pooling with two inner boundary pools. Across four datasets and six frozen encoders, SRDP improves mean balanced accuracy by 5.68 percentage points over native token averaging across 24 settings, including 11.22 points on average for CoNIC and Lizard. SRDP converts a coarse frozen PFM lattice into a mask-aligned, fine-grained cell representation without updating the encoder.
