title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

title: Robust Well-Log Reconstruction Across Point Gaps and Whole Wells via Boundary-Gated Soft-Thresholding Kalman Fusion
abstract: Missing wireline logs hinder subsurface characterization. Deep reconstruction networks suffer from gap-boundary steps and cross-basin shifts, while interpolation and Gaussian smoothers struggle with long intervals and outliers. We propose boundary-gated soft-thresholding Kalman fusion (ST-KF), unifying multiresolution wavelet shrinkage, distance-gated residual prior learning, and closed-form robust Kalman smoothing with learning--inference decoupling. Across two public benchmarks totaling 263 wells in the Norwegian North Sea and New Zealand's Taranaki Basin, ST-KF ranks first over 0.15--100-m anchored gaps with 0.09% parameter overhead. Against the strongest of nine baselines, pooled RMSE falls by 5.0%--8.3% for bulk density and 6.4%--15.6% for compressional slowness; against the four strongest baselines, reductions are 0.7%--4.1% for neutron porosity and 1.3%--2.9% for photoelectric factor. Ablations and sensitivity analyses confirm operator synergy and stable performance: removing state-space fusion increases short-gap errors by up to 58.8%, while zero-shot transfer cuts anchored errors by 14%--68%. The results show that local borehole continuity transfers across basins whereas cross-property mappings shift with regional geology, supporting measurement-guided log reconstruction.

title: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control
abstract: Problem definition: Inventory decisions select which demand enters sales logs. Unrecorded forecasts can leave demand frequencies unidentified even when stocking levels are recorded. We study which multistage ordering decisions these logs can justify and what finite samples can guarantee. Methodology/results: Nested stockout thresholds yield exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation. We choose one deterministic inventory rule to minimize its largest expected cost gap from the informed optimum under the same law. This population value is data debt for the specified information and policy class. Under independent demand, carryover can create positive debt despite common optimal actions in every isolated period. Finite samples add learning error above debt. The required sample count grows linearly with the selection bound, with upper and lower orders matching up to logarithmic factors. This rate requires fixed demand and cost bounds, sufficient revelation, and a uniformly positive probability of clearing all feasible stock across the confidence sets. Controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy improvements from tighter guarantees. Managerial implications: More records can tighten guarantees while debt persists. Deeper revelation can establish common optimality without fully identifying demand. Using these guarantees requires validated logging, a credible selection range, and a regret tolerance in cost units. Information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.

title: CARTA: Self-Supervised Reusable Transaction Embeddings via Heterogeneous Tokenization and Cross-Attention
abstract: Acquiring fraud labels for payment transactions is expensive and inconsistent across tasks, and high-cardinality identifiers such as merchant names make one-hot feature pipelines infeasible at scale. We present CARTA, a self-supervised encoder that learns a compact 16-dim embedding from raw transactions without labels; the frozen embedding is then reused for label-efficient fraud probing and exploratory unsupervised risk stratification without retraining the encoder. CARTA uses type-specific projections with learned embedding tables for high-cardinality identifiers, trained with token excision and InfoNCE contrastive loss. On IEEE-CIS, its linear probe at 1% of labels exceeds a raw-feature probe at 100%; on IBM TabFormer (2M rows), its frozen embedding reaches GBDT AUPRC 0.508, above frequency encoding (0.411) and the merchant-dropping baseline (0.022), though fully-supervised CatBoost is stronger. CARTA is a label-free, reusable representation that complements task-specific supervised models.

title: Well-Log Reconstruction with Pre-trained Geological Knowledge: A Knowledge-Conditioned Large-Language-Model Generative Agent
abstract: Missing well-log intervals make subsurface reconstruction ill-posed. Existing numerical regression models lack geological prior knowledge to constrain ambiguous inverse mappings. We propose GeoLog-Agent, a knowledge-conditioned generative agent using pre-trained large language models (LLMs) as a source of geological priors. A universal Geo-Harness translates LLM stratigraphic reasoning into formation-anchored petrophysical trajectories, feature-wise linear modulation, and conditional adversarial constraints. On the Norwegian North Sea benchmark, GeoLog-Agent achieves a mean $R^2$ of 0.9307 and a peak $R^2$ of 0.9713. It exceeds the nine-baseline average $R^2$ of 0.8387 by 0.0920, with a 30.97% average RMSE reduction, and exceeds the strongest baseline by 0.0274--0.0498 in $R^2$, with 16.25%--24.05% lower RMSE. Ablations confirm the effectiveness and synergy of geological prior reasoning, multi-scale dilated generation, and conditional adversarial modules. Transferring the coupling mechanism to six conventional deep learning models improves their $R^2$ by 0.0162--0.0789 with cross-well stability. These results demonstrate how foundation-model domain reasoning can constrain deep generative reconstruction of missing petrophysical measurements.

title: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
abstract: Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

title: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors
abstract: Hard vision benchmarks often keep images that strong classifiers get wrong. Since a classifier is also marked wrong when the label is wrong, such failure screens may collect label errors. We measure this on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set with 103 classifiers. Among the 1,892 images that all 66 supervised classifiers get wrong, 61% have a wrong label, versus 11.1% overall. The fewer images a screen lets through, the more of them are mislabeled, along approximately one curve. Fit on one model family, this curve predicts the screens of two held-out model families with a mean error of 2.4 percentage points, and replays of ImageNet-D's and ImageNet-Hard's screens within 0.1 and 6.3 points. title: Data-Driven Heuristic-Guided Business Process Redesign
abstract: Business process redesign (BPR) has a long-standing catalog of best-practice redesign heuristics, yet, applying them remains a mostly manual task that requires extensive domain knowledge. Despite recent advances using Large Language Models (LLMs) for conversational process model redesign, limitations remain. For example, redesign is user-driven instead of data-driven and is not guided by best practices such as the redesign heuristics. Moreover, only one change can be handled at a time. To address these limitations, given an event log and a BPMN model, we present the DH-BPR framework to realize data-driven heuristic-guided BPR using LLMs. To design DH-BPR, we first conducted an analysis of which redesign heuristics can be automatically detected and applied given information contained in an event log such as the fraction of cases that bypass an activity. Based on this, DH-BPR detects and validates heuristic candidates through a combination of rule-based techniques and an LLM. After that, DH-BPR jointly designs and records an application plan for valid candidates, before finally yielding a redesigned BPMN model and an updated resource model (the way resources execute the process). Evaluation based on simulation using a synthetic benchmark and two real-world event logs shows that the framework's redesign reduces the mean case completion time by up to 61.5%.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
abstract: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

title: More Context, Mixed Results: Evaluating LLMs for Identifier Recovery and Code Deobfuscation
abstract: Source code is often obfuscated through identifier renaming, incentivizing reverse engineers to develop techniques for recovering meaningful names. To assess how LLMs compare with these techniques, we evaluate 4 traditional baselines and 3 LLMs (Qwen, OLMo and DeepSeek) on identifier detection and semantic recovery across 51 recent Java projects, 3 obfuscators, and 6 context/retrieval settings. LLMs generally outperform traditional techniques on both tasks, but benefit from different forms of context and settings: agentic retrieval yields the strongest detection results, reaching 91.56% $F_1$, while enclosing-class context generally improves semantic recovery at a higher token cost. Despite these gains, exact recovery peaks at 16.42% overall (under one-hop context) and 32.93% for field names (under repository retrieval), which are the easiest to recover. Class identifiers are the hardest to detect, with a mean detection $F_1$ of 48.48% across models, settings and obfuscators. More context is not always beneficial: larger methods hinder semantic recovery. Beyond identifier renaming, our experiments show that control-flow obfuscation degrades both tasks more than string encryption. Our findings provide useful ad hoc insights for reverse engineers choosing models and context strategies to deobfuscate code snippets.

title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content
abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.

title: SAR-TopoGuard: Training-Free, Speckle-Aware Topological Verification for Structure-Preserving SAR-to-Optical Translation
abstract: SAR-to-optical translators often synthesize detail that the radar measurement does not support, and pixel metrics alone cannot reveal it. We propose SAR-TopoGuard, a training-free inference-time layer for frozen generators: a stochastic sampler draws K candidates (Monte Carlo dropout for GANs, seed variance for diffusion), a speckle-aware verifier ranks them by gradient-magnitude correlation with the SAR input and a hallucination-frequency index, and a SAR-guided frequency gate admits high-frequency detail only where SAR edges support it. With all five hyperparameters frozen and three training seeds, we evaluate on 500 scene-disjoint SEN1-2 test patches, 500 patches of a held-out summer scene, and 200 cross-dataset SEN12MS winter pairs. The layer improves Pix2Pix by +0.060, +0.012, and +0.077 dB PSNR and by +0.0034, +0.0057, and +0.0135 SSIM, respectively (Wilcoxon p < 1e-6), and it improves CycleGAN and CUT on all three sets (+0.013 to +0.076 dB). It raises edge precision at the cost of edge recall (edge F1 -1.3% on the test set). On the latent diffusion model COP-GEN, it adds +0.33 dB (base) and +0.16 dB (Beta) on the winter set, the only set with dual-polarization SAR. An ablation shows that the gate produces the gain for MC-dropout GANs, whose candidates are nearly identical, whereas verifier selection contributes up to +0.26 dB for diffusion, whose samples differ. The layer has zero trainable parameters and adds 0.4 ms per patch beyond the K=5 generator passes.

title: Understanding the Role of Reasoning Data in Pretraining
abstract: Reasoning data expose models to multi-step reasoning, but reasoning traces may cover only a subset of the available facts. How should pretraining balance atomic facts with reasoning traces? We study this question by constructing a setting in which every fact provides an atomic training signal, while only a subset appears in reasoning supervision, enabling us to measure generalization to transitions observed atomically but never used in training traces. For a linear transformer, we derive the weight assigned to atomic training signals that minimizes held-transition squared error and show that its leading-order optimum increases with reasoning-chain length and decreases with the fraction of facts held out from reasoning traces. These trends persist in a full transformer layer with an MLP, softmax attention, and cross-entropy loss. We further validate the role of reasoning complexity and data coverage in two natural-language settings: controlled multi-hop reasoning and mathematical pretraining. Together, our results provide a principled view of how reasoning-chain structure and data coverage should shape the allocation of training data during pretraining.

title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
abstract: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > β$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.

title: 具身智能动作决策的最小证据边界 / Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents
abstract: 本稿为中文方法与理论研究草稿,提出以当前动作是否可被证据确认,作为进一步获取观测的停止条件。稿件区分静态离线最短证书与在线自适应查询代价,并给出基本推导、动态失效反例与后续比较实验方案。研究仍处于探索阶段,新颖性与实际工程收益尚未建立;本文不是经同行评审的期刊论文。 Minimal Evidence Boundaries for Action Decisions in Embodied Agents. This Chinese-language methods and theory draft studies action-specific evidence acquisition, distinguishing offline certificates from online adaptive query costs. It includes elementary propositions, a dynamic invalidation counterexample, and a falsifiable evaluation plan. Novelty and practical benefits remain to be established. This is an exploratory preprint, not a peer-reviewed journal article. Validation is limited to a four-bit static logical model: 16 worlds, 81 partial-evidence states and 256 compatible world/evidence pairs. The included standard-library Python program and actual JSON output reproduce these checks. There are no physical robot experiments, learned-model benchmarks or claims of real-world safety. Query-count comparisons apply only to the stated toy model and uniform distribution. Files: six-page Chinese manuscript PDF, editable DOCX, Python checker, actual enumeration results and reproduction instructions. Manuscript version completed on 2026-11-13; repository publication date is 2026-11-14. The manuscript's statement that it had not yet been submitted describes its status when written. AI assistance was used for ideation, literature discovery, drafting, formalization, coding and typesetting. Related work and limitations are explicitly discussed. The listed author and affiliation follow author-provided information: YANGZHOU, 梗必爆具身交互AI研究院 (Genbibao Embodied AI Research Institute), ORCID 0009-0005-4736-2097. This record does not assert journal acceptance or indexing by CNKI or Scopus.

title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
abstract: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. title: A Backdoor Trigger Is Legible in Fine-Tune Weights
abstract: A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.

title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

title: Coverage Beats Chronology: Distilling Tabular Foundation Models for Drifting, Rare-Event Financial Risk
abstract: Distilling a tabular foundation model (TFM) into a CPU-deployable tree is established practice on IID benchmarks, where retention of the teacher’s absolute accuracy exceeds 95%, but financial risk breaks that setting twice over: the data are temporally ordered, and a gradient-boosted baseline is strong enough that the teacher’s edge is only an increment, so absolute retention stays high even when nothing useful transfers. We therefore report gain retention, Rgain, the fraction of the teacher’s advantage over a matched labels-only student that survives compression, and we factorially vary the one choice a practitioner must make: how the teacher’s soft targets are built. On frozen test windows of five temporal fraud streams (Bank Account Fraud with two bias variants, IEEE-CIS and Elliptic), a student scoring a row in 0.52 ms on one CPU core (107 × the teacher’s batched throughput) retains 96% of the teacher’s incremental advantage at a 16K-label budget (+ 8.7 pp PR-AUC). The decisive design choice is target coverage, not chronology: on BAF’s development window, labelling every available row is worth + 3.03 pp against + 0.50 pp for the construction protocol, and forward chaining, the temporally cautious scheme most practitioners reach for, is unnecessary and costs up to 3.5 pp; on frozen test windows the coverage advantage holds in all four replication streams (median + 0.97 pp over 12 cells). That advantage is conditional, and we quantify the condition: across 12 frozen-test stream–budget cells it grows with the teacher’s margin over a matched labels-only tree (r = 0.79), and where a tree already matches the foundation model the selector discards the teacher in 10 of 12 runs, making the choice moot by construction. The calibration cost that appears to accompany distillation is an artifact of temperature-scaled targets, not a property of the teacher, and inverts at no cost to ranking.

title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
abstract: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at https://github.com/Hamza-Kamil/NAP-WAVE.

title: Does Lifestyle Information Improve Hypertension Prediction? A Leakage-Controlled Evaluation on NHANES
abstract: Does readily available lifestyle information improve machine-learning prediction of hypertension beyond routine demographic and anthropometric data? On NHANES 2017-March 2020, five model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagged Decision Trees, and XGBoost) were evaluated with fold-local preprocessing and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Adding physical activity, alcohol use, smoking, and sleep information showed no consistent detectable improvement in held-out discrimination: every paired ROC-AUC confidence interval included zero, including under a stricter measured-blood-pressure phenotype and without synthetic oversampling. Mean cross-model SHAP rank agreement fell from 0.873 to 0.806 over all encoded columns, but this decline was largely attenuated over the 19 baseline columns shared by both arms (0.873 vs. 0.863), and likewise under both robustness checks; attribution-agreement comparisons across feature sets of different sizes therefore require a matched comparison space. In exploratory analysis of untreated adults (measured-blood-pressure outcome), all five models showed small positive differences, two with unadjusted intervals excluding zero, meriting confirmation. These results do not imply that lifestyle factors are clinically unimportant; within this cohort, the evaluated lifestyle block added little incremental discrimination beyond an already-informative baseline.

title: Beyond Controllability: Speaker Diversity in Instruction-Guided Text-to-Speech
abstract: Instruction-guided text-to-speech (ITTS) lets users specify voice properties in natural language. Applications from conversational AI character voices to synthetic training data for downstream speech models depend on the system producing many distinct voices when the same broad category is requested repeatedly. No prior work audits whether ITTS outputs are in fact diverse, either compared to real speech or across attribute values. We evaluate seven open-source ITTS systems using speaker embeddings whose representational capacity we independently validate. Every system produces speaker distributions markedly narrower than real speech. Furthermore, female prompts produce less diverse voice pools than male prompts across most systems. In contrast, accent and emotion prompts barely alter speaker diversity in most systems, but reveal a strong controllability bias toward North American English and neutral speech. These results show that diversity and controllability capture complementary weaknesses, neither of which alone is sufficient to evaluate ITTS. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/dlion168/ITTS-Speaker-Diversity.

title: A Governance Control-Plane for Agentic AI in Regulated Financial Systems: A Fraud-Detection Case Study
abstract: We propose a governance control-plane for agentic AI in regulated financial services: an agent-agnostic layer combining a bounded-autonomy policy engine, a hash-chained audit trail, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate, a dual-signal drift monitor (PSI + chi-squared), a kill switch, and a structured evidence-faithfulness check. Two findings stand out. First, confidence-based PSI completely misses a prompt-induced behavioral shift in Llama 3 while a post-hoc chi-squared decision-proportion test localizes the shift within 80 transactions of injection – empirical motivation for the dual-signal design, although online detection of this failure mode remains open. Second, 51% of escalations breach the 90-second SLA under realistic reviewer latency, motivating a re-queue policy that reduces permanent holds by 76.3%. Against a fail-open ungoverned baseline, the governed system raises recall from 49.1% to 92.6% (stability confirmed across 20 seeds); live Llama 3 validation achieves F1 0.928–0.949 without parameter recalibration. The faithfulness check catches 100% of controlled fabrications and 21% of real LLM magnitude-drift hallucinations. All mechanisms are mapped to EU AI Act, OCC, and MAS obligations. Code is released at https://github.com/researcher-4795/governance-control-plane.

title: Synthetic Neurosymbolic Task Generation with Controlled Constraint Complexity
abstract: We introduce NeSySy, a synthetic generator for neurosymbolic learning tasks that jointly produces logical constraints and consistent datasets. Unlike existing benchmarks, NeSySy provides fine-grained control over key properties such as constraint structure, tightness, input dependence, and data generation and alignment strategies. In particular, it allows the use of rich constraints over infinite domains, and uses solvers to ensure that the constraints are meaningful and that generated samples satisfy the constraints. We design NeSySy to support both learning with declarative constraints and learning from distant supervision. Across a range of constraint families, we provide evidence that its parameters induce systematic and largely independent effects on task difficulty. Using NeSySy, we study constraint-aware learning methods, identifying regimes where explicit constraint enforcement is beneficial and where expressive unconstrained models can instead learn constraint structure directly from data. Our results establish NeSySy as a controlled testbed for analysing the interaction between learning and logical structure. NeSySy is built around a pipeline that incorporates solvers. Satisfiability checkers (CNFgen and Z3) generate and certify constraints. Constrained optimizers (RC2 for MaxSAT, Z3 for OMT) compute optimal repairs that guarantee every generated sample is consistent.

title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

title: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation
abstract: Surveys help researchers keep up with fast-moving fields, but they take weeks to months to write. Automated survey generation (AutoSurvey) can alleviate this situation, but it is challenging to draw on hundreds to thousands of precisely scoped papers, choose among many valid structures, and stay faithful to its sources while offering insights. We present SurveyWeave, an agentic architecture that decomposes the problem into four tasks coordinated by three agents, each reviewing others' work and conducting revisions based on feedback. We also introduce WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys. A comprehensive comparison shows that SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points.

title: Beyond skin deep: physiologic oral pigmentation as an overlooked validation gap in AI-assisted oral cancer screening
abstract: AI-assisted oral cancer screening tools, exemplified by MeMoSA, have been validated almost exclusively in Asian populations. We propose a testable hypothesis: physiologic oral pigmentation, which varies by race independent of pathology, may cause classifiers to misclassify normal variation as suspicious or miss camouflaged lesions. Following precedent from pulse oximetry and dermatology AI, we call for pigmentation-stratified validation before deployment in racially diverse settings such as the United States.

title: Learning Spatially Aware Audio-Visual Features from Videos with Mono Audio
abstract: Comprehensive audio-visual perception requires both semantic and spatial reasoning. Existing spatial models suffer from poor generalization due to data scarcity, while semantic-only models fail to capture spatial characteristics completely. We introduce a model capable of jointly reasoning over binaural audio and vision on semantic and spatial tasks with improved generalization. To overcome the shortage in real-world data, we develop an automatic pipeline that localizes the sound source in a video, estimates its relative 3D trajectory, and renders binaural audio. We then use this to spatialize VGGSound, allowing us to train at a much larger scale. We demonstrate improved performance and generalization on spatial reasoning tasks while still remaining competitive on semantic tasks compared to semantic-only models.

title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
abstract: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

evidence.title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
evidence.abstract: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

title: When Errors Have Unequal Consequences: Second-Order Complementary Log Loss for Cost-Sensitive Boosting
abstract: Multiclass decisions in finance can have sharply asymmetric consequences: reserving nothing for a loan that subsequently liquidates can be much more costly than reserving too much for a loan that repays. Standard softmax cross-entropy depends only on the probability assigned to the true class and does not encode these decision costs. We address this gap by building a cost matrix into the training loss: each possible wrong decision has its own penalty term, scaled by the consequence of that decision under the true outcome, so a decision is penalized by its estimated impact rather than by the bare fact that it differs from the true class. We adopt cost-weighted complementary log loss ( cwcl ), an established loss with a potentially asymmetric cost matrix, as an objective for second-order gradient-boosted trees. Our central contribution is its second-order treatment: the exact raw-logit gradient and diagonal Hessian, a proof of non-convexity in the logits, and a numerically stable implementation with a non-negative Hessian approximation. We also prove that the population minimizer’s highest-scoring action minimizes expected cost under the supplied matrix; cwcl ’s outputs are decision scores, not calibrated class probabilities. We evaluate loan-loss reserve decisions on 60, 176 seriously delinquent loans from Freddie Mac’s Single-Family Loan-Level Dataset, covering 2011–2015 origination vintages and a 2017 test year. We score on each loan’s subsequently realized loss. Across five training seeds, cwcl assigns a zero reserve to around 3 of the 1, 528 test loans that later liquidate, against around 29 for a direct cost regression that is trained on each loan’s own realized losses rather than on class labels. cwcl ’s mean loss is \(0.15\%\) of exposure below calibrated cross-entropy with the minimum-expected-cost decision and \(0.24\%\) above the direct regression. On a public eight-class life-insurance benchmark, cwcl gives up some accuracy and probability quality but reduces ordinal cost by \(10.1\%\) relative to cross-entropy with standard multiclass arg-max settings. These findings characterize the optimization and decision trade-offs of complementary-log boosting within the evaluated methods.

title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
abstract: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.

title: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
abstract: An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

title: Semantic Credibility: Cold-Start Priors for Novel Insurance Claim Codes with LLM Embeddings
abstract: New insurance claim codes enter portfolios before code-specific outcomes are available. Classical credibility then falls back to a collective or observed parent-group estimate, leaving families absent from training undifferentiated. We introduce Semantic Credibility (SemCred), a nested estimator whose lowest rung is a code-specific prior constructed from outcomes of description-similar training codes. Family gates operate in both severity and volume channels; an own-experience gate is used only for severity, where independent claim counts support an automatic transition toward code experience. Volume remains a cold-start prior in the absence of an exogenous exposure denominator. We evaluate synthetic ICD-9 claims and real Medicare HCPCS payments using unseen-code holdouts with the family represented in training and unseen-family holdouts, hierarchy-composition tests, and a four-fold rolling backtest. Against pre-specified matched-depth fallbacks, SemCred lowers severity and expenditure log-MAE in all four dataset-regime conditions; this comparison isolates the semantic rung rather than claiming dominance over deeper hierarchies. When inserted beneath stronger prefix or ontology structures, the semantic rung matches or improves standalone accuracy, with the largest gains where hierarchy is empty or weak. A SapBERT ladder achieves temporal severity error of 1.268 versus 1.492 for hierarchical credibility, and 1.27 versus 1.51 on codes officially activated in the target year. SemCred is a traceable lower rung for code-level payment priors whose severity component retires as claims accumulate. The code is available at: https://github.com/yejining99/semcred

title: Fairness Evaluation for Diffusion and Flow Models Should Account for the Generation Path: Implications for Clinical Imaging
abstract: Medical image generation models are often evaluated using images produced by a single sampling procedure. However, diffusion and flow models can use different numbers of sampling steps, sampling schedules, or numerical solvers without changing their trained parameters. These changes may affect the generated images and the clinical measurements derived from them. We argue that fairness results obtained under one sampling procedure should not be assumed to hold under another, particularly when changes in sampling affect clinical task errors differently across patient groups. Building on previous work on medical image quality, accelerated sampling, generation dynamics, and generative model fairness, we examine why the sampling procedure should be considered part of the evaluated system. We define subgroup differences in clinical task error across sampling procedures and provide a mathematical example showing that two groups can have identical outputs under the exact dynamics and a reference sampler but different errors under an alternative sampler. We also extend this result to stochastic generation under shared noise. An exploratory experiment with an age-conditioned image generation model illustrates how changing the number and timing of sampling steps can alter image-derived measurements, although these differences do not establish clinical unfairness. We therefore argue that fairness evaluation should assess the sampling procedure used in practice and examine intermediate generation states when they help explain differences in clinically relevant errors across patient groups. Analysis code is available here https://github.com/rdharini2001/generation-path-fairness

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

title: Phoenix Experiment — Grok image interactions dataset (v1.0)
abstract: A small, descriptive dataset of public exchanges on X in which the author's accounts (@BJ_Beyond, @BJ_hal) addressed @grok and an image generated by Grok appeared in the exchange. It documents a ritual convergence: over a few days Grok's image replies settled into a fixed, slot-based text template carrying author-introduced keywords. The dataset describes what was observed; it does not establish a mechanism. Window: 5 Aug – 13 Nov 2026 (53 rows), plus 2 pre-window rows (19 Apr and 1 May 2026) for context only. 55 rows; 51 Grok replies with media; 2 self-declared rows; 58 unique images. Times in Europe/Rome; latency = Grok reply time minus user post time. Limitations. Photos only: exchanges without an image are not included, so there is no denominator and no trigger rate can be estimated. Small n: 53 in-window rows over 9 days. 2 rows are self-declared Grok-made images whose prompt is not public. Human authorship of the prompts is the account owner's testimony (14 Nov 2026) and cannot be verified via the API. "Rule six" is the author's own convention, not a documented Grok or xAI feature. Statements produced by Grok are model output (claims to test), not findings. The finding is descriptive; any mechanism is a hypothesis. Part 2 (vessel test, exit, extinction) is pending. What is not included. Grok images and Grok's full reply texts are not redistributed and are not covered by the CC BY 4.0 license. Posts are referenced by X Post ID and official x.com URL; images by the SHA256 checksum of the copy archived privately by the author.

title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
abstract: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

title: 标题:卦象层:一种基于《易经》二进制编码的离散瓶颈架构及其移动端验证 Title:Hexagram Layer: A Discrete Bottleneck Architecture Based on the Binary Encoding of the Book of Changes and Its Mobile Verification
abstract: 大模型连续隐状态缺少显式结构约束,容易引发语义漂移与逻辑不一致;《易经》六十四卦作为完备的6位64状态符号系统,长期局限于哲学解读,缺少可训练、可复现的计算实证。本文提出卦象层,一种融合周易卦象二进制编码的离散瓶颈可微架构。首先将六十四卦映射为6位二进制状态,对错卦、综卦、互卦、变卦四类卦变操作给出严格形式化定义,借助邻接矩阵构建卦变状态转移约束;其次提出爻象结构化初始化策略,为原型向量注入卦象先验偏置,替代传统随机初始化;推导得到结构先验有效性、判别边界迁移充分条件、粗粒化信息单调性三条理论定理。在Android移动端基于纯C++标准库完成全部前向、反向逻辑实现,不依赖深度学习框架,开展三组对照实验。实验结果表明:爻象结构化初始化能够显著加速离散瓶颈层判别边界迁移;不满足学习率充分条件时模型无法收敛;粗粒化变换符合信息单调不增规律;迭代互卦映射时观测到由既济、未济二卦构成的周期‑2极限环,该现象与《易经》以两卦收束全篇的文本特征存在观察层面的呼应。本文为传统符号文化的计算化实证提供一套可复现的实现范式。 Abstract The continuous hidden states of large‑scale models lack explicit structural constraints, which may lead to semantic drift and logical inconsistency. As a complete symbolic system with 6 bits and 64 states, the sixty‑four hexagrams in the Book of Changes have long been limited to philosophical interpretation, lacking trainable and reproducible computational evidence. This paper proposes the Hexagram Layer, a differentiable discrete‑bottleneck architecture integrated with binary encoding of I‑Ching hexagrams. Firstly, the sixty‑four hexagrams are mapped to 6‑bit binary states. Four hexagram‑transformation operations, namely inverse hexagram, reversed hexagram, mutual hexagram and changed hexagram, are formally defined, and hexagram‑transition constraints are constructed via adjacency matrix. Secondly, a hexagram‑structured initialization strategy is proposed to inject hexagram‑based prior bias into prototype vectors instead of conventional random initialization. Three theoretical theorems are derived concerning the validity of structural prior, sufficient conditions for decision‑boundary migration, and information monotonicity of coarse‑graining. All forward and backward computations are implemented purely in C++ standard library on Android mobile devices without deep‑learning frameworks, and three groups of comparative experiments are carried out. Experimental results demonstrate that hexagram‑structured initialization greatly accelerates decision‑boundary migration of the discrete bottleneck layer; the model fails to converge when the sufficient condition of learning rate is violated; coarse‑graining transformation satisfies the monotonic non‑increase property of information. A period‑2 limit cycle formed by Ji‑Ji and Wei‑Ji is observed during mutual‑hexagram iteration, which is observationally consistent with the textual feature that the Book of Changes ends with these two hexagrams. This work provides a reproducible paradigm for computational verification of traditional cultural symbols.

evidence.title: 标题:卦象层:一种基于《易经》二进制编码的离散瓶颈架构及其移动端验证 Title:Hexagram Layer: A Discrete Bottleneck Architecture Based on the Binary Encoding of the Book of Changes and Its Mobile Verification
evidence.abstract: 大模型连续隐状态缺少显式结构约束,容易引发语义漂移与逻辑不一致;《易经》六十四卦作为完备的6位64状态符号系统,长期局限于哲学解读,缺少可训练、可复现的计算实证。本文提出卦象层,一种融合周易卦象二进制编码的离散瓶颈可微架构。首先将六十四卦映射为6位二进制状态,对错卦、综卦、互卦、变卦四类卦变操作给出严格形式化定义,借助邻接矩阵构建卦变状态转移约束;其次提出爻象结构化初始化策略,为原型向量注入卦象先验偏置,替代传统随机初始化;推导得到结构先验有效性、判别边界迁移充分条件、粗粒化信息单调性三条理论定理。在Android移动端基于纯C++标准库完成全部前向、反向逻辑实现,不依赖深度学习框架,开展三组对照实验。实验结果表明:爻象结构化初始化能够显著加速离散瓶颈层判别边界迁移;不满足学习率充分条件时模型无法收敛;粗粒化变换符合信息单调不增规律;迭代互卦映射时观测到由既济、未济二卦构成的周期‑2极限环,该现象与《易经》以两卦收束全篇的文本特征存在观察层面的呼应。本文为传统符号文化的计算化实证提供一套可复现的实现范式。 Abstract The continuous hidden states of large‑scale models lack explicit structural constraints, which may lead to semantic drift and logical inconsistency. As a complete symbolic system with 6 bits and 64 states, the sixty‑four hexagrams in the Book of Changes have long been limited to philosophical interpretation, lacking trainable and reproducible computational evidence. This paper proposes the Hexagram Layer, a differentiable discrete‑bottleneck architecture integrated with binary encoding of I‑Ching hexagrams. Firstly, the sixty‑four hexagrams are mapped to 6‑bit binary states. Four hexagram‑transformation operations, namely inverse hexagram, reversed hexagram, mutual hexagram and changed hexagram, are formally defined, and hexagram‑transition constraints are constructed via adjacency matrix. Secondly, a hexagram‑structured initialization strategy is proposed to inject hexagram‑based prior bias into prototype vectors instead of conventional random initialization. Three theoretical theorems are derived concerning the validity of structural prior, sufficient conditions for decision‑boundary migration, and information monotonicity of coarse‑graining. All forward and backward computations are implemented purely in C++ standard library on Android mobile devices without deep‑learning frameworks, and three groups of comparative experiments are carried out. Experimental results demonstrate that hexagram‑structured initialization greatly accelerates decision‑boundary migration of the discrete bottleneck layer; the model fails to converge when the sufficient condition of learning rate is violated; coarse‑graining transformation satisfies the monotonic non‑increase property of information. A period‑2 limit cycle formed by Ji‑Ji and Wei‑Ji is observed during mutual‑hexagram iteration, which is observationally consistent with the textual feature that the Book of Changes ends with these two hexagrams. This work provides a reproducible paradigm for computational verification of traditional cultural symbols.

title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
abstract: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

title: Faithful by Audit: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness in Financial Decisions
abstract: Financial decision systems pair a tabular classifier with post-hoc feature attributions, typically SHAP over gradient-boosted trees. They report which features affected the score, not why a decision was made. Large language models can generate chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations, but fluent rationales need not be faithful. We study two high-stakes financial settings: transaction fraud detection and consumer credit risk, where the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) requires accurate adverse-action reason codes. Using LoRA fine-tuning, distillation, and DPO with faithfulness-based preferences, we construct CoT explainers for IBM TabFormer and LendingClub, and audit them with FinFaith, a unified intervention-based auditing suite. Three findings replicate across both domains. First, on identical evaluation subsamples, XGBoost consistently outperforms all CoT variants; therefore, we argue that CoT is an explanation layer, not a replacement scorer. Second, observational faithfulness is easy and interventional faithfulness is hard. The models cite features fluently and compute their arithmetic correctly 60–98% of the time, yet perturbing a cited feature changes the decision barely, more often (credit) or less often (fraud), than perturbing a feature the CoT never mentions. Third, a planted geographic cue drives up to 40% of CoT explainers’ credit decisions, yet disclosure is 0% among cases it demonstrably flipped. Faithfulness training raises interventional sensitivity, necessity from 8% to 54%, add-mistake sensitivity from 5% to 42%, but broadly rather than selectively toward what the CoT cites, and leaves the disclosure gap unclosed (cue reliance rises from 2.5% to 40.2% while confession stays at 0%). Hence, we conclude that faithfulness must be treated as an audit gate, not an assumed property, before CoT is used as a financial explanation.

title: Generate, Align, and Restore: MLLM-Empowered Diffusion for Generalizable Low-light Image Enhancement
abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is essential to numerous vision applications operating under adverse illumination. Despite substantial advances, real-world nighttime enhancement remains challenging due to the scarcity of strictly aligned day-night pairs and complex degradations involving extreme darkness and heterogeneous artificial light sources, leading to fragile generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose MrLIE (MLLM-empowered reference Low-light Image Enhancement), a novel reference-based unsupervised LLIE framework that synergizes the generative and reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with conditional diffusion. MrLIE employs the MLLM as a high-fidelity reference synthesizer and diagnostic critic, iteratively generating, diagnosing, and correcting normal-light references directly from degraded nighttime observations. Based on this, our method governs the enhancement process through two complementary mechanisms, in which a confidence offset module rectifies spatial-geometric inconsistencies for reference reliability and a structure-anchored injection scheme harmonizes aligned reference cues, low-light structural constraints, and ControlNet additive anchoring during the denoising process. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that MrLIE achieves superior perceptual quality, natural appearance, and robust generalization.

title: Consistency-Aware Map Generation at Multiple Zoom Levels Using Aerial Image
abstract: The multi-level tiled map service is widely used and serves as a kind of digital infrastructure. These map tiles are usually rendered from vector data, whose update needs to walk or drive with professional equipment to check every points of interest. This leads to inconvenience and expensive cost in timely updating maps. Compared with vector data, aerial images are much easier and cheaper to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel multi-level map generation framework that can automatically generate accurate and consistent maps with multiple zoom levels from aerial images. It consists of a level-aware map generator and a consistency-aware map generator. The level-aware map generator is able to generate accurate initial maps with realistic details for each zoom level. The consistency-aware map generator regards initial maps at each zoom level as a sequence and builds the connection between them, so as to guarantee content consistency between maps at different zoom levels. Furthermore, we collect a large-scale high-quality dataset called Multi-Level Map (MLM) for map generation at multiple zoom levels. Experiments on our MLM dataset show that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art map generation methods on both comprehensive quantitative metrics and perceptual quality.

title: LC-ISP Benchmark: Learning Advanced ISP with Live and Capture Streams
abstract: High-quality paired RAW-to-sRGB datasets are essential for data-driven ISP, yet existing datasets often rely on cross-device collection, causing misalignment and failing to faithfully reflect real capture conditions. We therefore introduce LC-ISP, a large-scale benchmark built from the intrinsic gap between a camera's live preview and offline capture streams. LC-ISP contains 53.9k spatially aligned groups, each comprising live RAW/live sRGB and multi-frame fused RGB/capture sRGB, and covers day, night, indoor, outdoor, and HDR scenes. It also provides capture-stream intermediates for modular supervision. We further develop a compact two-stage baseline that uses these intermediates as auxiliary targets. Under a 2.5-GFLOP budget for 448$\times$448 RAW inputs, it outperforms the strongest single-frame baseline by over 2 dB PSNR while improving texture, denoising, and color reproduction. LC-ISP supports realistic benchmarking, the design of supervision strategies, and the development of lightweight ISP models.

title: Evasión robusta de un clasificador comercial de detección de IA mediante un sistema generador propietario: evidencia experimental preliminar
abstract: Se evaluó, bajo protocolo de caja negra, un sistema generador de texto desarrollado íntegramente por el autor y denominado internamente Barthes Pseudomonádico KD45, frente a Pangram 4.1 — clasificador comercial de detección de texto sintético, de uso extendido en los flujos editoriales, académicos y periodísticos, y operado de forma independiente al autor. El sistema evaluado produjo tres muestras en español clasificadas con confianza del 100% como “Human Written” (n = 198, 210 y 216 tokens léxicos). Como condición de contraste, dos muestras generadas por un modelo de lenguaje de propósito general sobre premisas narrativas de complejidad equiparable fueron clasificadas con confianza del 100% como “AI Generated” (n = 377 y 324 tokens), en la misma sesión de evaluación y sin mediar ningún procedimiento de post-edición sobre ninguna de las dos condiciones. Se reporta esta discrepancia con evidencia documental directa (capturas de pantalla del clasificador) y se discuten sus implicaciones para la literatura de detección adversarial de texto sintético. Por razones de estrategia de protección de propiedad intelectual y de una eventual transacción de licenciamiento, el método generativo se reporta exclusivamente como caja negra: no se caracteriza su arquitectura, su espacio de hipótesis, ni se confirma o descarta el uso de ninguna familia de técnica conocida en la literatura de generación de lenguaje natural.
