title: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
abstract: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. We instead propose a DFL framework that achieves risk-sensitive behavior while retaining point predictions and deterministic optimization at inference time. Starting from the dual representation of the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) and adding entropy regularization, we derive a smooth surrogate for the CVaR of regret. Its gradient induces an instance-dependent reweighting within each minibatch that emphasizes high-risk outcomes, so the approach can turn existing surrogate-loss DFL methods, including the SPO+ loss, into risk-sensitive variants. When instantiated with SPO+, the resulting objective admits a generalization bound on the CVaR of the true regret. Experiments on knapsack, portfolio, shortest-path, and energy-aware scheduling problems show substantial reductions in tail regret when the uncertain parameters exhibit heterogeneous tail behavior.

title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

title: AlphaLeak: What `Blind' LLM Trading Benchmarks Still See
abstract: Benchmarks often describe an LLM evaluation as blind after replacing company names and tickers with anonymous identifiers. We argue that blindness is not a preprocessing operation but an empirical property: under a declared threat model, the released record must resist linkage to its source while retaining what the benchmark means to evaluate. Our matched utility–linkability audit for point-in-time stock ranking holds the stock, date, numeric features, and realized return fixed, varying only the visible identity and news representation. An open-ended LLM, given one name-masked record (Blind) and neither a candidate list nor a corpus, names the issuer on 71% of rows; with same-date corpus access, fixed retrieval attacks recover the source on 99.8% of rows, and strict redaction, typed entity replacement, and LLM rewriting remain similarly linkable. Theme and Event abstractions cut exact-stock recovery to 5.1% and 3.9% against a 1.37% chance rate, but neither improves the Rank Information Coefficient over a numeric-only condition, so no tested representation combines near-chance linkability with detectable utility. Raw news is model- and prompt-order-sensitive and statistically unresolved within sectors; its sample portfolio difference concentrates in sector allocation without establishing within-sector selection. Separate attacks recover identity from numeric profiles and longitudinal scores even when text is masked. These surfaces motivate a threat-model-relative complete-record audit reporting source and group linkability and no-news-anchored, target-level utility. The code is available at https://github.com/minsuk-sung/ICAIF2026-AlphaLeak.

title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

title: Beyond Clumsy Agentic Tool Calling: How Cueing and Spotting Make the Difference
abstract: LLM-based task-oriented agents depend on tools to interact with their environments, but may overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist with unproductive strategies. These behaviors can hinder agents' ability to use tools autonomously and sustain task progress. We characterize tool-use symptoms at two temporal granularities: local clumsy tool-use behaviors and tool-use detours spanning multiple interactions. Towards greater autonomy in tool use, we present ToolPulse, an online middleware supporting autonomous tool use through cueing and spotting. ToolPulse tracks execution state and temporal interaction patterns, monitoring proposed calls before dispatch and inspecting execution feedback prior to the agent resumes reasoning. It combines state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to identify intervention opportunities and provide verbal reminders, structured feedback, or context-specific advice from auxiliary models. Our process-oriented evaluation distinguishes trigger validity, behavioral cessation, and substantive correction alongside task outcomes and resource costs. Using SWE-agent with three backbone models, we evaluate 1,350 trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks, comparing unassisted execution with four assistance strategies. Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for tool-use detours. Concise reminders achieve the highest observed aggregate substantive-response rate; more elaborate assistance offers symptom-dependent benefits and can be less effective. Aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings. These findings support proactive runtime assistance for autonomous tool use. The gap between behavioral adjustment and aggregate repair gains calls for careful decisions on intervention timing and assistance strategy in autonomous agents.

title: FAP-Bench: A Matched-Control Benchmark for Horizontal Federated Cross-Sectional Equity-Return Prediction
abstract: Institutions that each hold part of the equity market’s history cannot pool it. FAP-Bench measures what they give up by training a return-prediction model together instead, exchanging model updates and, to standardize inputs, monthly aggregate histograms. It is a controlled laboratory for horizontal federation rather than a model of any particular consortium. It prices the coordination cost of that restriction, not the privacy it buys: clients are stylized industry splits of one licensed panel, and privacy is priced at a single differential-privacy setting. The benchmark builds a 3.27M firm-month panel from CRSP and Compustat over 1964–2023, splits it into twelve industry clients, and runs centralized, local-only and three federated rules at a matched compute budget. Every configuration publishes the smallest gap it can resolve before any method is ranked, and every heterogeneity treatment is paired with a control that imposes the same aggregate burden evenly, so the difference isolates cross-client structure. Two findings. First, a coordination cost appears in the one configuration where the model resolves more signal. On seven characteristics, where the network resolves little signal, no rule separates from pooling economically. On twenty, where the model resolves substantially more signal, the two averaging rules give up accuracy that the cell does resolve (Rank IC, q < 0.02). They also show a net Sharpe shortfall that it does not resolve, which we report as a bound. An adaptive server optimizer stays level with pooling on both, but its server step size was searched and the pooled model’s optimizer was not, so this does not show that it matches an equally tuned pooled model. Both configurations resolve gaps of comparable size, so this is a difference in effect, not in power. Two configurations cannot establish a trend, and they differ in panel width, network size and client learning rate at once, so the cost cannot be attributed to any one of these. Swapping the network for ridge also changes which rule pays, so no ranking among the rules holds across model classes. Second, heterogeneity in what a client holds clears the benchmark’s noise floor, while heterogeneity in how it participates almost never does. The participation side is measured mostly on 60 test months, where our intervals are somewhat too narrow, and only one of its three treatments is rechecked on 408. Most economic differences sit below what this data can resolve, so we report magnitudes as bounds rather than estimates.

title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.

title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.

title: Evasión robusta de un clasificador comercial de detección de IA mediante un sistema generador propietario: evidencia experimental preliminar
abstract: Se evaluó, bajo protocolo de caja negra, un sistema generador de texto desarrollado íntegramente por el autor y denominado internamente Barthes Pseudomonádico KD45, frente a Pangram 4.1 — clasificador comercial de detección de texto sintético, de uso extendido en los flujos editoriales, académicos y periodísticos, y operado de forma independiente al autor. El sistema evaluado produjo tres muestras en español clasificadas con confianza del 100% como "Human Written" (n = 198, 210 y 216 tokens léxicos). Como condición de contraste, dos muestras generadas por un modelo de lenguaje de propósito general sobre premisas narrativas de complejidad equiparable fueron clasificadas con confianza del 100% como "AI Generated" (n = 377 y 324 tokens), en la misma sesión de evaluación y sin mediar ningún procedimiento de post-edición sobre ninguna de las dos condiciones. Se reporta esta discrepancia con evidencia documental directa (capturas de pantalla del clasificador) y se discuten sus implicaciones para la literatura de detección adversarial de texto sintético. Por razones de estrategia de protección de propiedad intelectual y de una eventual transacción de licenciamiento, el método generativo se reporta exclusivamente como caja negra: no se caracteriza su arquitectura, su espacio de hipótesis, ni se confirma o descarta el uso de ninguna familia de técnica conocida en la literatura de generación de lenguaje natural.

title: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
abstract: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. We show the discounted plug-in approach finds an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with $O(SA (1-γ)^{-3} \varepsilon^{-2} \log(SA/δ))$ samples, where $S, A, γ, δ$ are the state and action sizes, discount factor, and failure probability, respectively. In the average-reward setting, we show that discounted plug-in and direct (undiscounted) plug-in achieve $O(SAH\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ and $O(SAD\varepsilon^{-2}\log(SA/δ))$ complexities, respectively, where $H$ upper-bounds the optimal bias span and $D$ is the diameter. Combining with our lower bounds for nonadaptive generative models, these results resolve the minimax sample complexity of discounted RL and average-reward RL --- in both the span- and diameter-based classes --- up to constant factors. Our main technical contribution is a novel Bellman residual bracketing technique which improves the efficiency of prior absorbing-MDP-based concentration analyses.

title: Neylira-Φ: Recurrent Optimization Curves and Certified Recursive Learning - Sharp Thresholds, Exact Finite-Observation Limits, and Compositional Certificates for AI Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki
abstract: Neylira-Φ is a self-contained mathematical research monograph connecting the geometry of optimization trajectories, fundamental limits of finite observations, and structural certificates for accepted changes to a learning system. This release contains the complete 81-page expanded manuscript, including 48 pages devoted to AI recursive self-improvement, together with editable LaTeX, reference implementations, exact rational and symbolic verification programs, figures, audit records, and structured research data. The central question is how to distinguish apparent progress from a mathematically certified improvement in a learning procedure. A decreasing loss curve can repeatedly violate discrete convexity, and even exact finite loss-and-gradient observations can fail to determine whether those violations will persist indefinitely. Nevertheless, explicit assumptions on update operators, task comparisons, evaluation procedures, and computational costs can certify particular modifications. The manuscript develops both sides of this distinction: impossibility results for observation alone, and constructive guarantees for structurally certified changes. 1. Sharp recurrence for constant-step gradient descent For every normalized constant step h = eta*L satisfying 7/4 < h < 2, the manuscript constructs a globally smooth, strongly convex scalar C(1,1) objective with a convergent gradient-descent trajectory and infinitely many strictly negative second differences of the objective values. Here C(1,1) means continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz gradient. The construction has an exact scaled return. With the minimum normalized to zero, a period P and contraction factor 0 < R < 1 satisfy: x[k+P] = R*x[k] f(x[k+P]) = R²*f(x[k]) At infinitely many designated indices: f(x[k]) − 2*f(x[k+1]) + f(x[k+2]) < 0 Thus the objective remains strongly convex and the loss decreases, while the sequence of loss values repeatedly fails discrete convexity. The exact return identity establishes persistence over infinitely many cycles. The universal convexity theorem for h ≤ 7/4 is established prior work, reproduced with attribution to Barzilai, Shamir, and Zamani. Together with that lower-range theorem, the construction gives the sharp recurrence-existence boundary within the stated strict stability interval. The manuscript also distinguishes regularity classes. Under the specified positive-definite linearization and strict stability assumptions, differentiability of the gradient at the limiting minimizer forces eventual recovery of loss-curve convexity. Analytic approximations can preserve arbitrarily long prescribed finite patterns of violations. This does not assert infinite recurrence for one analytic objective under a constant gradient step. 2. Exact finite observations do not identify the eventual regime An explicit quadratic-core patch modifies the objective in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of its minimizer. Two compensating moment conditions preserve both function values and gradients outside the modified core. For every prescribed finite exact observation transcript of the recurrent construction, an eventually recovering companion can therefore match that transcript while preserving the declared smoothness and strong-convexity bounds, minimizer, minimum value, and initial gap. The quantifiers matter: each finite transcript admits a suitable companion; a single recovering objective is not claimed to match the entire infinite recurrent orbit. In the stated promised family and exact point-oracle model, this yields impossibility results for always-terminating deterministic classifiers and almost-surely finite randomized classifiers, including procedures with adaptive query locations. Randomization does not provide a worst-case success guarantee strictly above one half over the entire family. These results concern finite point observations; symbolic descriptions and additional structural assumptions can supply information beyond that oracle model. 3. A necessary and sufficient criterion for arbitrary positive-definite switching For positive-definite quadratic tasks, the manuscript derives an exact universal loss-curve convexity criterion for arbitrary symmetric positive-definite optimizer switching. The normalized update matrices may fail to commute; simultaneous diagonalization is not assumed. If their spectra lie in [a,b], with 0 < a ≤ b < 2, define: rho = max(abs(1−a), abs(1−b)) nu = distance from 0 to the interval [1−b,1−a] Gamma = 1 − rho²*(2 − nu²) Universal loss-sequence convexity in this class holds if and only if Gamma ≥ 0. The bounds concern the energy-normalized update matrices. A strict positive margin supports the stated local nonlinear extension under the required remainder and domain conditions. An explicit analytic example with alternating step sizes shows why the equality boundary Gamma = 0 cannot generally inherit that nonlinear guarantee. The manuscript also supplies an exact recurrent construction with noncommuting updates outside the admissible switching region. 4. Exact burst lengths and asymptotic event densities For the contraction-ratio model E[k+1] = q[k]*E[k], where q[k] lies in [a,b] and 0 ≤ a ≤ b < 1, the manuscript determines the largest possible number of consecutive strict negative second differences and the maximal asymptotic frequency of those events. Define: Delta = 1/(1−b) − 1/(1−a) M = max(0, ceil(Delta) − 1) The exact maximum consecutive burst length is M, and the maximal asymptotic event density is M/(M+1). Explicit periodic constructions attain both bounds. The strict integer boundary is part of the result. These theorems classify the declared contraction-ratio model. They do not claim to solve the optimal consecutive-violation geometry of every fixed-step gradient-descent problem. A scalar-quadratic corollary gives exact burst thresholds under bounded relative-gradient errors. 5. Constructive progress observers and task interpretation Every Schur-stable linear update map admits a computable positive-definite observer with any prescribed finite order of positive alternating differences. The construction selects an observer for the requested finite order; it does not require one observer to control every order simultaneously. The manuscript gives finite computation procedures, nonnormal examples, perturbation budgets, and extensions to the stated nonlinear and changing-map settings. Established Lyapunov and hypercontraction ideas are attributed. A comparison bridge connects observer-energy control to an external task, making explicit what must be established before internal progress implies protected-task improvement. 6. Compositional guarantees for accepted recursive improvements The 48-page recursive self-improvement part develops a conditional mathematical framework for changing optimizers, representations, objectives, and evaluation procedures while tracking accumulated errors and costs. If accepted changes satisfy: v[j+1] ≤ r[j]*v[j] + d[j] their exact propagated certificate is: v[N] ≤ (product of r[j] for j = 0,...,N−1)v[0]+ sum over i = 0,...,N−1 ofd[i](product of r[j] for j = i+1,...,N−1) An empty product equals 1. This expression separates contraction from approximation error, representation-transfer error, and objective drift. Further results connect changing internal certificates to a fixed protected residual, give retention bounds for task families, and describe when the accumulated guarantee remains meaningful. Fresh-data, anytime-valid promotion tests and inherited error budgets control false promotions across indefinitely many adaptive proposals under the stated conditional-validity assumptions. A claim that every committed version improves protected population utility requires evidence covering every commitment. The framework guarantees properties of accepted changes satisfying its assumptions; it does not guarantee an unlimited supply of beneficial proposals. 7. Computational benefit includes proposal and validation costs The manuscript separates iteration-count improvements from improvements in actual work. A certified target-time advantage requires an upper work bound for the candidate, including proposal and evaluation overhead, below a lower work bound for the baseline from the same checkpoint to the same target. An exact worked example reduces total assigned work from 66 to 40 units, including 20 units of proposal and validation overhead. For a less demanding target, the same modification instead costs 28 units against the baseline’s 22. These calculations demonstrate a precise payback condition within an explicit mathematical cost model. They are theoretical cost comparisons; practical neural-network speedups require measurement. Research significance The manuscript provides a mathematical connection between observational nonidentifiability and constructive certification of self-modification. It identifies what a finite training history cannot establish and specifies additional conditions under which individual learning-system changes can be accepted with compositional guarantees. Potential applications include learning-curve interpretation, optimizer selection, protected-task retention, adaptive evaluation, and research on certified recursive learning. The contribution combines explicit constructions, sharp classifications in declared models, and conditional certificate composition. Applying the framework to large neural networks requires evidence that its assumptions and cost comparisons hold in those systems. Verification and reproducibility All 11 supplied finite audit programs and the executable example printed in the manuscript passed in the original reproduction record and in a fresh packaging run on a disposable copy. Fresh-data, anytime-valid promotion tests and inherited error budgets control false promotions across indefinitely many adaptive proposals under the stated conditional-validity assumptions. A claim that every committed version improves protected population utility requires evidence covering every commitment. The framework guarantees properties of accepted changes satisfying its assumptions; it does not guarantee an unlimited supply of beneficial proposals. 7. Computational benefit includes proposal and validation costs The manuscript separates iteration-count improvements from improvements in actual work. A certified target-time advantage requires an upper work bound for the candidate, including proposal and evaluation overhead, below a lower work bound for the baseline from the same checkpoint to the same target. An exact worked example reduces total assigned work from 66 to 40 units, including 20 units of proposal and validation overhead. The contribution combines explicit constructions, sharp classifications in declared models, and conditional certificate composition. Applying the framework to large neural networks requires evidence that its assumptions and cost comparisons hold in those systems. title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

title: dit.xpu : Taming DiT Sparse Inference on Mobile SoCs
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.

title: Perfilado Epistémico y Señales Honestas Costosas: Hacia una Metodología Forense
abstract: Authorship attribution and the profiling of anonymous actors in complex digital and forensic environments are undergoing an irreversible epistemological crisis. Traditional methodologies—grounded in lexical and syntactic stylometry, code analysis, infrastructure metadata, and temporal patterns—prove deeply vulnerable against adversaries equipped with high operational security (OPSEC) discipline. This paper posits that digital forensics, open-source intelligence (OSINT), and criminal analysis must abandon low-friction indicators (when confronting sophisticated adversaries) as these belong to the economic category of "Cheap Talk." As its core methodological contribution, this article introduces the framework of Epistemic Profiling driven by Costly Cognitive Signals (Cognitive Proof-of-Work). Grounded in the Handicap Principle from evolutionary biology, information economics, and computational cryptography, the model contends that the key to attribution lies not in the generic amount of knowledge required, but in deciphering the actor’s theoretical framework, mental heuristics, and problem-solving system. By auditing how an individual decomposes, approaches, and resolves a challenge under pressure—demonstrating that an actor linked to a specific educational, generational, and/or cultural background will solve the exact same problem in a characteristic and structurally distinct manner from another, regardless of using identical contemporary tools—the analyst isolates the traces of an inalienable "doctrinal ecosystem." This enables the construction of a rigorous educational, institutional, and geographic profile of an anonymous actor, both in exploratory investigative scenarios and in filtering processes across bounded sets of candidates.

title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
abstract: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

title: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
abstract: Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) systems can lose intelligibility in noise environments because they cannot adapt to environmental changes. However, humans tend to increase their vocal efforts in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. Building on an auditory-feedback Lombard TTS, we investigate whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS can learn acoustic adaptation directly from auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feedback and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback are extracted from the noise-corrupted waveforms and injected into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates. We assess feedback benefits across prompting and noise conditions using plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired-finetuning. Experiments show that while finetuning provides strong robustness under in-domain conditions, auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise. Moreover, stronger power/F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.

title: Finite-Sample Recovery of Predictive History Quotients from Independent POMDP Trajectories
abstract: We study a modest but identifiable abstraction problem for partially observed control: under one fixed data-collection policy, which bounded observation contexts have the same finite-horizon continuation law? We define the *episode-position predictive quotient*, an explicitly policy- and position-dependent estimand. Our estimator first selects contexts on one half of independently reset trajectories, then takes at most one prespecified continuation block from each trajectory in the other half. It compares fixed- alphabet histograms by empirical total variation and abstains whenever a pair lacks the samples required by its own concentration bound. Under an $`\varepsilon`$-gap, a per-context visitation floor, and a selection threshold no larger than the inference threshold, we prove exact recovery with probability $`1-\delta`$ from $`O((d+\log(K/\delta))/(\mu_{\min}\varepsilon^2))`$ trajectories, where $`d`$ is the continuation-alphabet size and $`K`$ the selected context count. A two-point construction shows the dependence on $`\mu_{\min}`$ and $`\varepsilon`$ is unavoidable; the dependence on $`d`$ is not matched and is known to be improvable by optimal closeness testers. The guarantee is non-asymptotic: it does not treat overlapping windows as independent, does not rely on chi-square calibration, and conditions each context only on its own count, so nested candidate contexts are covered. Implementation checks on three analytically solvable environments—each with $`\varepsilon`$ set below its known gap—recover the exact quotients on all of 20 seeds, including an environment whose quotient requires merging; a budget sweep shows the power gate degrading through abstention with no incorrect merge at any budget; and a position-nonstationary chain shows the overlapping-window mode systematically merging contexts the episode-position quotient separates.

title: Read, Then Shade? How Visual Evidence Changes Incentive-Driven Misreporting in Vision-Language Advisors
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly read a scene and report it to someone who acts on the report, sometimes under objectives that differ from that person's. We ask whether a stated incentive moves what a VLM reports, and whether this changes when the value must be read from pixels rather than given as text. In seeded synthetic scenes, a model reads the position of a target on a labelled axis and reports one integer to a fixed receiver; it is paid, in simulation, for accuracy or for a report a few units to one side, and every scene is also presented with the true value as text. Across a pilot and three follow-up studies with hash-frozen protocols, four small open VLMs from three families, and 15,170 held-out trials, a stated payoff moved reports in both modalities, and exact compliance at three units was significantly lower with the image than with text for three of four models; Qwen2.5-VL 7B showed no reliable difference. Adding the true value as text to the image prompt removed the gap in every model. For InternVL3 the gap vanished on scenes it read correctly when it wrote its reading first; for Gemma 3 it persisted. For Qwen2.5-VL 3B, which read every scene correctly, the gap held in four of five payoff paraphrases, nearly vanished when the model wrote its reading before its report or when the prompt stated that the client wants the truth, vanished with an unpaid goal, and persisted when the model reported before stating its reading; how often it shaded at all, even with text, depended strongly on the wording. When told that the client wants the true value, three of four models still shaded every text report. Visual input did not make these advisors reliably more truthful; it made compliance with a stated incentive depend on whether the read value is made explicit and on output order, a dependence that text-only evaluations and mean-shift metrics do not reveal.

title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

title: SemMask: Semantic-Prioritized Progressive Masking for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) are designed to enable globally parallel generation. However, in practice, they often exhibit pseudo-autoregressive behavior and a function-word-first bias, which undermines their performance on tasks such as text writing and code generation that benefit from global planning and parallel decoding. To address this, we propose SemMask, a novel fine-tuning paradigm that leverages a semantic-prioritized progressive masking strategy to encourage the model to decode high-information semantic tokens early and globally, thereby enhancing its global planning and parallel generation capabilities. Specifically, we first use the gradients of the original DLM with respect to each token to identify semantic tokens. During masking, these semantic tokens are preserved with priority, establishing a progressive generation order in which semantic tokens are decoded prior to function tokens. Meanwhile, we adjust the loss weight for semantic tokens to further reinforce their early prediction. Experimental results show that SemMask achieves quality comparable to strong autoregressive baselines on both text writing and code generation tasks, while providing superior semantic coherence. Notably, SemMask achieves higher accuracy with substantially fewer decoding steps, indicating that the early establishment of semantic structure improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off.

title: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
abstract: The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

title: Don’t Trust, Verify: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Engineering for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Feature engineering in tabular fraud detection is critical yet challenging to automate due to extreme class imbalance, which heavily penalizes spurious features. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate candidate features from dataset schemas, schema-level plausibility correlates poorly with actual predictive value. We propose an LLM-based Automated Feature Engineering (AutoFE) framework that assesses candidates strictly on executed empirical behavior. Every candidate is executed on a data split to extract a structured profile of empirical metrics, including deterministic data-integrity checks and output value distributions. A role-separated multi-agent panel, comprising a Critic, Proposer, and Adjudicator, evaluates this evidence to rigorously retain, repair, or discard features. Because the optimal interpretation of raw diagnostics is unknown a priori, a single evaluation pass is insufficient. To bridge this gap, a validation-gated meta-learning stage optimizes the system iteratively across multiple execution passes. By analyzing the realized downstream utility of previously accepted features, this stage dynamically refines the natural-language skills used to read diagnostic tools, updates system memory regarding feature-family behavior, and recalibrates acceptance thresholds for subsequent passes. Evaluated on three severely imbalanced fraud benchmarks (CCF, TabFormer, BAF v2), our framework achieves the strongest PR-AUC among the evaluated LLM-based methods while retaining compact feature sets. By consolidating the evaluation process, moving from iterative, trial-and-error prompting to a single, comprehensive diagnostic profile, the method reduces per-pass evaluation costs by 42% while significantly lifting predictive performance, including a PR-AUC increase from 0.878 to 0.949 on the CCF dataset.

evidence.title: Don’t Trust, Verify: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Engineering for Financial Fraud Detection
evidence.abstract: Feature engineering in tabular fraud detection is critical yet challenging to automate due to extreme class imbalance, which heavily penalizes spurious features. While Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate candidate features from dataset schemas, schema-level plausibility correlates poorly with actual predictive value. We propose an LLM-based Automated Feature Engineering (AutoFE) framework that assesses candidates strictly on executed empirical behavior. Every candidate is executed on a data split to extract a structured profile of empirical metrics, including deterministic data-integrity checks and output value distributions. A role-separated multi-agent panel, comprising a Critic, Proposer, and Adjudicator, evaluates this evidence to rigorously retain, repair, or discard features. Because the optimal interpretation of raw diagnostics is unknown a priori, a single evaluation pass is insufficient. To bridge this gap, a validation-gated meta-learning stage optimizes the system iteratively across multiple execution passes. By analyzing the realized downstream utility of previously accepted features, this stage dynamically refines the natural-language skills used to read diagnostic tools, updates system memory regarding feature-family behavior, and recalibrates acceptance thresholds for subsequent passes. Evaluated on three severely imbalanced fraud benchmarks (CCF, TabFormer, BAF v2), our framework achieves the strongest PR-AUC among the evaluated LLM-based methods while retaining compact feature sets. By consolidating the evaluation process, moving from iterative, trial-and-error prompting to a single, comprehensive diagnostic profile, the method reduces per-pass evaluation costs by 42% while significantly lifting predictive performance, including a PR-AUC increase from 0.878 to 0.949 on the CCF dataset.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
abstract: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title: Size-Matched Nulls Reveal What Block Ablation Measures in MambaVision
abstract: Hybrid vision backbones interleave Mamba state-space mixers with self-attention, and a block's role is usually probed by removing it and measuring the damage. We test what that measurement means in MambaVision. On all 50,000 ImageNet validation images and three model sizes, every block ablation is paired with a size-matched null, the same perturbation with its channels shuffled or their signs flipped. In top-1 accuracy and in true-class rank, real and null damage are nearly indistinguishable in absolute terms: pooled over the blocks of MambaVision-T, the content effect lies within [-0.044,+0.016] percentage points (90% interval). Two attention-only controls show that the test detects content, with real ablations worse than their nulls by up to 4.2 points in DeiT-Small and 1.0 point in Swin-T. Part of MambaVision's near-equivalence reflects how little damage its blocks do (0.11--0.34 points on average, against 1.7 and 2.1). Scaled by damage, its content share is comparable to Swin-T's in accuracy, lower in rank, and far below DeiT-Small's: single-block damage in MambaVision is small and mostly positional. Ablation also hides what blocks carry together: removing all blocks of one type compounds damage to 3.7--8.4 times the sum of single effects, far more than size-matched nulls, including nulls that keep the alignment between the blocks' perturbations; for adjacent pairs, aligned nulls reproduce most of it. Freezing input-dependent selection in all Mamba mixers shows that it accounts for 20--32% of the Mamba contribution, mainly through the B and C projections. We turn these results into a protocol for causal attribution in hybrid networks.

title: The Alert-Feedback Trap: Why Drift-Adaptive Fraud Detectors Fail Under Realistic Label Feedback, and How Much Exploration It Takes to Escape
abstract: Financial-crime detectors must adapt to drift, but in deployment they are retrained almost entirely on the labels their own alerts produce: only flagged transactions are investigated and labeled. We characterize the resulting failure mode, the alert-feedback trap. On the Elliptic Bitcoin dataset, detectors across linear, tree-ensemble, and graph-neural-network families collapse under a regime change (illicit-class F1 from 0.91 to 0.03), though ranking degrades far less than fixed-threshold metrics suggest. Under alert-only feedback, drift-adaptive learners that update from a recent window of alert-selected labels are trapped: a strong detector that catches 113 of 169 illicit transactions while frozen falls to 93 when it adapts on its own alerts—worse than freezing in all 200 bootstrap resamples and under every gate setting we tried—and a collapsed detector recovers only 9–30, versus 98 under bulk feedback. The trap is an interaction of selection bias and forgetting, not an inevitability of alert-only feedback: a practitioner baseline that retrains on the full label history plus the alert labels escapes it under the same feedback (113 → 130; collapsed 14 → 79), while the same alert labels without the history do not (74; 46). Off-policy ϵ -exploration, by contrast, is not a reliable escape once data variability is accounted for. We release a prequential protocol with delayed, budgeted, selection-biased feedback.

title: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent
abstract: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.

title: Lesion-Aware Explainable AI for Diabetic Retinopathy Grading from Fundus Images
abstract: Post-hoc explanations of deep-learning models for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading are difficult to trust because different attribution methods highlight different retinal regions for the same image, and a visually plausible heatmap does not show that the highlighted pixels drive the prediction. We propose the Consensus-Calibrated Explanation Map (CCEM), which fuses Grad-CAM++, Ada-SISE, and SmoothGrad Integrated Gradients (SG-IG) using image-specific weights derived from annotation-free reliability cues: deletion sensitivity, inter-method agreement, compactness, retinal containment, and peak structure. CCEM explains a frozen ordinal grader, an EfficientNet-B7 with CBAM and a scalar regression head, pre-trained on EyePACS 2015 in Stage 1 and fine-tuned on APTOS 2019 in Stage 2 with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)-optimized thresholds; it reaches a QWK of 0.920 on the hidden Kaggle test set and 0.559 on the external MAPLES-DR cohort. Explanations are evaluated on MAPLES-DR, 198 MESSIDOR images with expert pixel-level lesion annotations that are never used for training, threshold fitting, or fusion. On the 193 images with annotated lesions, CCEM obtains the highest Soft Pointing Game score (69.61%; 95% CI 63.7-75.3), defined as the ratio of the strongest lesion-supported saliency to the global map maximum rather than a lesion detection rate, together with the lowest deletion AUC (0.570) and the best deletion-insertion balance (0.115); each gain is significant against the strongest single explainer on paired tests. Annotation-free, per-image reliability weighting therefore turns three disagreeing explainers into one map whose peak evidence is more lesion-supported and more faithful to the model than that of any single explainer.

title: BINA Theory: A Four-State Conceptual Framework for Information Representation
abstract: BINA Theory is a four-state conceptual framework for representing information, evidence, and evaluation. It defines four distinct symbolic states: -1 (Opposed or Rejected), -0 (Unknown or Insufficient Evidence), 0 (Neutral), and 1 (Supported). Its central distinction is that -0 and 0 represent different informational conditions. This record documents the foundational definitions and currently established symbolic representation of the framework. This is a foundational conceptual record, not a claim of experimentally verified superiority or a completed formal logic system.

title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
abstract: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

title: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents act on repositories through shell commands and file edits, and teams steer them with written engineering rules. Industrial settings expect such rules to be enforced and their application to be evidenced, and a rule given as prompt text provides neither. We test whether executable contracts enforced while the agent works reduce rule violations compared with the same rules in the prompt, retrieved as guidance, or checked only after generation. Violations are scored by an oracle whose methods differ from the in-loop checks, and the oracle is validated by two human reviewers and a model reviewer. Across three studies on two model families (240, 112 and 108 runs), enforcement during execution produced no oracle-detected violation in 104 paired runs, against 21 to 55% of runs without rules, and no loss of functional correctness in the two confirmatory studies. In the confirmatory study on tasks aimed at known failure situations (Study 3, protocol hashed before the first run), enforcement lowered the share of violating runs by 31 percentage points relative to no rules (Holm-adjusted p = 0.014); the 17-point difference from prompted rules was not significant (p = 0.12), and neither was any contrast in Study 2, where only 3 of 14 tasks produced a violation. Prompted rules removed some violation types but not recursive deletes of scratch directories, and checks after generation repaired file edits but not commands that had already run. That enforcement satisfies the rules it enforces is expected by construction; what the data add is where prompting falls short, the absence of a functional cost, and the limits of the rules and of the oracle themselves. The studies use low-cost models and one small fixture.

title: CARGO: Credit Action Recourse via Regulation-Bounded, Graph-Constrained Ordered Planning
abstract: Lenders are required to disclose the principal reasons for a credit denial, and recent guidance asks that those reasons be specific enough to act on. This requirement points to recourse , the actionable steps that turn a denial into an approval. Existing explanation and recourse methods operate at the level of individual features. Attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME report influential features rather than actions an applicant can take, counterfactual methods compute feature changes that rarely map to real actions, responsiveness scores assemble no plan when no single feature responds, and none of them accounts for actions that depend on one another. We propose CARGO (Credit Action Recourse via Regulation-Bounded, Graph-Constrained Ordered Planning), which builds recourse from actions rather than individual features. CARGO fixes a catalog of credit actions matched to the reason codes lenders already file, arranges them in a constraint graph of precedence and exclusion edges with a per-applicant applicability filter, and searches for the ordered feasible plan most likely to reverse each denial. Disclosure practice reports at most four reasons per notice, and CARGO adopts this cap of four actions per plan. One plan then serves both audiences, executable recourse for the applicant and verified reason codes for the lender’s notice. In experiments on nine dataset–model cells, CARGO achieves the highest executable recovery on eight, raising it by up to 28.6 points compared to the best competitor while returning no infeasible plan, and recovers up to \(97\%\) of the applicants whom single-feature methods abandon. Ablations show that the action catalog and the constraint graph each contribute to this improvement.

title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
abstract: Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming. Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

title: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
abstract: Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer's joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user's recordings of other activities, or other users' recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as "more data" versus "less data," which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN-GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user's own data. A user's own other activities raise $R^2$ from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit-stand-walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users' same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity ($G_\mathrm{T} = +0.053$) and half as much once own other-activity data exist ($G_\mathrm{W} = +0.028$); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. title: CGGS: Confidence-Guided Graph Sampling for Scalable GNN Fraud Detection on Imbalanced Financial Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) offer a powerful paradigm for financial fraud detection by exploiting the relational structure of transaction networks to identify suspicious behaviour and coordinated fraud. Translating them into a viable production system, however, remains hard under strict memory, compute and latency budget – costs that span the entire model lifecycle, not merely GNN training. A real transaction graph of hundreds of millions of accounts is overwhelmingly a graph of benign nodes, so much of that lifecycle budget is spent processing nodes that carry little discriminative signal. The same benign majority drives a second challenge, fraud-class homophily collapse : because fraudsters deliberately interact with legitimate entities to camouflage and evade detection, the proportion of same-class edges incident on fraud nodes drops and the fraud class is driven into high heterophily, so neighbourhood aggregation averages the fraud signal away while imbalance biases the classifier toward the benign majority. We propose CGGS ( C onfidence- G uided G raph S ampling), a two-stage framework that turns both liabilities into a single opportunity at no additional compute cost. Stage 1 trains a lightweight tabular scorer – gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) in our instantiation – on the node features, ranking every candidate entity by fraud probability without touching graph topology. Stage 2 prunes the confidently-benign entities before the graph is assembled, so the GNN trains only on the compact, higher-homophily subgraph of uncertain, high-risk, and informative nodes. We prove that confidence-guided pruning increases the expected fraud-class homophily and reduces the effective imbalance ratio under a mild ranking assumption. Experiments on a production-scale proprietary transaction graph and two public benchmarks show that CGGS reduces graph size and lifecycle computational cost while outperforming full-graph training and alternative pruning strategies, with ablations confirming robustness across pruning thresholds.

title: Evidence-Conditioned Completion and Synthesis of Electronic Health Records
abstract: Patient information can guide electronic health record (EHR) generation, but how its amount shapes predictive utility and disclosure risk remains poorly characterized. Here we present EHRDiB, which unifies visit completion and synthesis by distinguishing original missingness from withheld inputs and combining a shared multimodal representation with an evidence-conditioned latent diffusion bridge. We compared EHRDiB with three completion and eight synthesis methods on MIMIC-IV and numerical and discretized Duke Health representations. Evaluation covered downstream predictive utility, generative diversity, and distributional fidelity for both tasks, and disclosure risk for synthesis. EHRDiB achieved the smallest utility gaps from real-data-trained classifiers in seven of eight completion comparisons. In synthesis, AUPRC gaps were 45.2% smaller for ten MIMIC-IV principal-diagnosis targets and 53.3% smaller for numerical Duke Health data relative to the best comparator. Synthesis with calibrated thresholding yielded the lowest marginal distribution error across all three datasets, with Coverage above 0.95 for both output rules. Across twelve evidence-fraction intervals in MIMIC-IV synthesis, membership-inference AUROC increased from 0.516 to 0.598 as the mean target evidence fraction rose from 0.20 to 0.50; utility gaps narrowed relative to the lowest evidence configuration but did not decrease monotonically. Our study provides a unified framework and empirical foundation for EHR generation that considers both its utility for clinical analysis and its information disclosure risk.

title: Auditable Authorization for LLM Agents: Empirical Evidence Across Model, Harness, and Workflow Layers
abstract: Human approval provides effective control only if rejected work stops and authorized work completes. We formalize refusal safety and bounded authorization completeness, and audit three execution boundaries: the model selects a call, the harness schedules and resumes it, and the workflow routes the decision to a protected effect. Paired decisions, exact traces, and native business-state witnesses support experiments with three models, five prompt arms, four runtime approval designs, two additional framework replays, and 100 public workflow sources. The paired model panel leaves seven of 300 approvals unfinished despite zero denied effects; parallel confirmation loses an approved branch in three tasks per model, restoration omits 336/672 CrewAI approvals, and four of 59 comparable n8n workflows execute after Reject. Comparing intent, generated calls, dispatch, and native effects identifies the first observable divergence and its repair target. This yields a practical audit contract that makes both refusal safety and authorization completeness independently verifiable, converting human approval from a procedural formality into an enforceable control boundary between intent and real-world effect.

title: Data and code for input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift in water-pollution incident classification
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript “Input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift: An evaluation of water-pollution incident classifiers”. This retrospective study evaluates 1,648 compiled incident records (2004–2024), retaining all four recorded severity grades: 1,375 minor, 188 moderate, 61 major and 24 exceptionally major records. The predictor audit restricts 27 candidate fields to 15 retrospective inputs. Evaluation includes grouped nested validation, three forward-time windows and two basin holdouts, with feature selection confined to training partitions. S1_Data_and_code.zip contains the original Excel snapshot, processed tables, field and duplicate audits, executable Python analysis, environment specifications, fold assignments, record-level predictions, feature-selection records, bootstrap outputs and figures. README_data_and_code.md describes reproduction, provenance and limitations. Archive size: 12,784,439 bytes. SHA-256: 2ef99d08ec200ac0376e3822e10183b3cd9729f706fbe8a1a7b22b4bb9396d01. An earlier source compilation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20426262. That record contains an older, different analysis and is not the archive of this four-level study. The present package preserves the new four-level analysis and its validation outputs. Limitations: original incident notices, complete meteorological product documentation and label-adjudication records are unavailable in the supplied compilation. Candidate incident groups are not verified unique event identifiers. Computational reproducibility does not establish the authenticity, accuracy or prospective availability of the original observations. This is not a validated emergency prediction product. Third-party dependencies and the TabICLv2 checkpoint retain their own licenses; model weights are not relicensed by this record. OpenAI Codex assisted planning, code, checking, visualization, interpretation and writing; no incident observations were generated. Authors remain responsible for verification and scientific claims. Authors: Ruidong Chen, Xin Zhao, Dapeng Deng, Yongmei Wang and Jie Tang, Anhui Agricultural University. Funding: National Key Research and Development Program of China (2023YFC3205701) and Cultivated Land Quality Big Data Platform Service Project (HX20250744), both awarded to Yongmei Wang. The authors declare no competing financial or non-financial interests.

title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.

title: Beyond Alignment: Supervising the Generator for EEG-to-Image Reconstruction
abstract: Visual brain decoding translates neural activity into human-interpretable images. While recent EEG-to-image reconstruction methods rely on aligning EEG signals with pretrained visual embeddings to condition an image generator, we empirically demonstrate that stronger cross-modal alignment do not translate into comparable gains in reconstruction quality. This indicates that improving the input condition alone is insufficient; the generative process itself requires explicit supervision. Although Representation Alignment (REPA) offers a solution by guiding diffusion transformers with pretrained vision encoder features, we find that EEG-conditioned generators struggle to follow these fixed targets. To address this mismatch, we introduce generation-derived supervision (GDS): an image-conditioned teacher that translates static image-encoder features into the internal representation space of a diffusion transformer. Our EEG-conditioned student generator closely tracks these dynamic targets during denoising, discarding the teacher at inference. Evaluated on THINGS-EEG and THINGS-MEG, our approach consistently outperforms conditioning-centric baselines, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Circuit Atlas
abstract: A living collection of small-network circuit studies for algorithmic tasks: hand-built reference networks, partly trained and from-scratch transformers, and external recurrent-model zoo snapshots. Entries report task performance separately from substitution and complement-resampling evidence, and keep failures, limited coverage and unresolved mechanisms. This archive holds the atlas text, figures and code; the networks and training snapshots are archived on Hugging Face at the revisions named in the release notes.

title: Analytical Examination of the Closed-Loop Oscillatory Hypothesis: Non-Monotonicity, Area Preservation, and Prime-Gap Jitter
abstract: Follow-up mathematical examination to Zenodo record 24026149. Establishes a formal definition of orbital learning, proves the impossibility of monotonic convergence in the frozen closed-loop architecture, and demonstrates exact local area preservation ($\det(J_n) = 1$) under prime-ratio feedback.

title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
abstract: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.
